whyPoints.description: Every dirham band here belongs to the provider that published it with the month read. No regulator approval, no UAE office, no grade guarantees, no invented statistics, and no assessment detail stated beyond what the school's own documents say.

faqs.question: Does it matter whether an MYP tutor is in Al Mankhool or the next district?
faqs.answer: No, and for this programme the comparison carries almost no information. MYP provision near these districts is concentrated in a small number of continuum schools rather than distributed, the nearest being over in Al Jaddaf, so students from Al Mankhool, Karama and Bur Dubai already travel to a handful of campuses. The tutor pool is shared across the whole belt and the published rates do not vary by street. The decisions worth your attention are about criteria, routes and comparisons, not geography.

faqs.question: My child's MYP grade has not moved despite a term of tutoring. Why not?
faqs.answer: Most often because the tutoring aimed at the wrong criterion. An MYP grade is a combination of band judgements against published descriptors, each assessing something different - knowledge, inquiry, communication, reflection. A student can genuinely improve their subject knowledge while the weak criterion remains weak, and the reported grade does not move. Ask the school for criterion-level feedback and the descriptor for the band above, then check whether the sessions were aimed at that specific difference or at the subject in general.

faqs.question: Is a criterion mark of 5 out of 8 roughly sixty per cent?
faqs.answer: No, and reading it that way causes most of the confusion in MYP households. A criterion mark is a band judgement against a published descriptor: a 5 describes a particular quality of work rather than a proportion of marks achieved. The consequence is that progress inside a band shows as no change at all, while a small targeted change can move a band immediately if it supplies exactly what the next descriptor asks for. Neither pattern makes sense if the number is read as a percentage.

faqs.question: Which MYP criterion is worth working on first if we only have one hour a week?
faqs.answer: Usually reflecting, then communicating. Reflecting is the fastest-moving criterion and the most neglected: students describe what they did where the descriptor asked them to evaluate what the work showed and what they would change, and that is one teachable move. Communicating responds nearly as fast, because it assesses structure and justified expression rather than knowledge. Knowing and understanding is the slow one - it accumulates over terms and cannot be shortcut, which is why aiming an hour a week at it often shows nothing.

faqs.question: How should we read an MYP report card across eight subject groups?
faqs.answer: Across the criterion rows rather than down the subject columns. If reflecting is weak in Sciences, Design and Arts simultaneously, your child has a reflection problem rather than three subject problems, and one block of work on evaluation language will improve three reported grades. That pattern is common and almost never noticed, because reports are read subject by subject. Where the weakness really is confined to one subject's content criterion, a term-long subject hour is the right purchase instead.

faqs.question: Should our child do the MYP or IGCSE to sixteen?
faqs.answer: Both are available near Al Mankhool, which makes this a real decision rather than an inherited one. IGCSE builds examination stamina and produces named qualifications that receiving institutions state requirements in. MYP builds investigation, design, reflection and independence, and prepares the Diploma's internally assessed components and Extended Essay unusually well while leaving a gap in timed examination technique. Neither is better; ask which gap is easier for this student to close later, and check what the receiving school requires by named qualification before deciding.

faqs.question: Which half of the Diploma does an MYP background actually prepare?
faqs.answer: Well on one half of it and less well on the other. MYP students arrive in Year 12 comfortable with criteria, internal assessment, independent project work and reflection - which is where a large share of Diploma difficulty actually sits, and where their IGCSE peers usually struggle. What they typically lack is examination stamina, because most MYP schools set no terminal papers. That gap is closable with deliberate timed-paper practice from the first term of Diploma year one, and it does not close by itself.

faqs.question: What is the Personal Project actually marked on?
faqs.answer: Planning, the application of skills and reflection - the documented process rather than the product. This is the thing most families get the wrong way round. A modest project with a rigorous process journal, clear success criteria set at the outset and honest evaluation against them, outscores an ambitious project whose journal was written retrospectively in a weekend. An experienced marker can see the difference. The habits also transfer directly into the Extended Essay and every Diploma internal assessment two years later.

faqs.question: How much help is allowed with the Personal Project?
faqs.answer: A clear amount, and no more. A tutor may explain what each criterion rewards, test whether a goal is achievable with the time and resources available, show what a process journal has to contain, read the student's own writing and question reasoning that does not hold, and point out where a section does not address its criterion. A tutor may not produce the project, write the journal or draft any part of the report. IB Gram tutors do not produce assessed work, and the consequences of the alternative fall on the student.

faqs.question: Does MYP Mathematics Standard or Extended matter for the Diploma?
faqs.answer: It matters for one specific route. The Extended route carries the additional algebraic depth that Diploma Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level assumes, so a student on Standard who later wants that course has a real gap. Analysis and Approaches at Standard Level and Applications and Interpretation at either level are reachable from the Standard route with ordinary preparation. The difficulty is timing: the route is usually settled in Year 9 or 10, before any Diploma view exists, so ask by Year 10 whether a move is still possible.

faqs.question: Our child moved into an MYP school at twelve and is struggling. What is wrong?
faqs.answer: Frequently not the content but how work is judged. A student arriving from a national or British primary curriculum meets criterion assessment for the first time, and nobody explains it to them in those terms. They produce work that would have scored well under a mark scheme and it sits in a middling band because the descriptor wanted something else - a justified decision, an evaluated outcome, a documented process. Two or three sessions on the descriptors themselves usually does more than a term of subject content.

faqs.question: Are MYP students assessed by examination at the end of Year 11?
faqs.answer: In most schools, no. Assessment is against the four criteria per subject group across the year, through tasks the school sets, with the Personal Project in the final year. Arrangements differ between schools, so confirm your own school's with the coordinator rather than assuming either way. The practical consequence for a family is that revision in the usual sense has little purchase: there is no single paper to prepare for, and the way to move a grade is to move a criterion on assessed tasks.

faqs.question: How much does MYP tutoring cost around Al Mankhool?
faqs.answer: Published Dubai rates start at AED 33 to 52 from Tutopiya and AED 45 to 65 from EdFlik, which can be reasonable where the weak criterion is content knowledge. Bestimate's 2026 Dubai table puts qualified online tuition at AED 150 to 300, with Unitors publishing IB tuition from AED 200, specialist IB provision at AED 200 to 450 or more, TutorChase at AED 270 and BartyED at AED 650. In-home including travel is quoted at AED 180 to 500. All read October 2026, all theirs rather than ours, and none varies by district.

faqs.question: Is the cheapest tier of tutoring ever the right choice for MYP?
faqs.answer: For one of the two cases, yes. Where the weak criterion is knowing and understanding in a subject with an ordinary curriculum base, competent general tuition at the budget end does real work and the specialist rate is overspend. What the examination-oriented end of this market cannot do is read a published criterion descriptor and aim at the band above it, because that requires familiarity with MYP assessment. For a reflecting or communicating block, buy a small quantity from somebody who knows the descriptors.

faqs.question: How many hours a week of MYP support are realistic in this district?
faqs.answer: One, occasionally two. MYP students from Al Mankhool and Bur Dubai travel to a continuum school, so their afternoons are shorter than their IGCSE neighbours', and eight subject groups produce assessed tasks on their own schedules through the year. Add the mandatory Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies periods inside the school day, calculated by KHDA on a forty-minute lesson unit, and the week is tighter than it looks. A plan built honestly around one well-aimed hour frequently succeeds.

faqs.question: Do you provide MYP descriptors, unit plans or exemplar work?
faqs.answer: No, and no provider should. Criterion descriptors, unit planners and exemplar material are published and owned by the IB, and your child's school holds the current versions and will share what it is permitted to. A tutor's work is to explain what a descriptor rewards, show the difference between one band and the next, and question the student's own work against it. If a provider advertises a library of IB assessment material as a selling point, ask who holds the copyright in it.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-al-mankhool.closingHeading: Ask for the descriptor, then aim at the gap
dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-al-mankhool.closingBody: The single most useful thing an MYP family can do costs nothing: ask the school for criterion-level feedback and for the descriptor of the band above the one your child is in. That difference is the target, and it explains why a hard-working student's grade has not moved. Read the report across the criterion rows rather than down the subject columns, because one weak criterion repeated across several groups is one problem rather than several. Then bring an assessed piece of your child's own work to a free trial lesson and let the descriptor set the plan. Sessions run one-to-one over live video.

intro.heading: The Middle Years year, counted backwards from the tasks that make the grade
paragraphs: Parents new to the Middle Years Programme often look for a syllabus and cannot find one in the form they expect. There is no single list of content ending in a terminal paper. Instead there are units, and inside each unit a summative task, and that task is marked against four criteria out of eight each. The grade on the report is built from those marks. Which means a Middle Years plan is not organised around topics at all. It is organised around dates.

That changes what tutoring should look like. A student whose next summative task is a scientific investigation needs different work in the next three weeks from a student whose next task is an extended written response in individuals and societies, even if both sit in the same year group at the same school in Mirdif. Working generically through the subject is the common mistake, and it produces a student who knows more and scores the same, because the criterion that was costing them marks was never addressed.

So the first thing a useful tutor asks for is not a textbook. It is the assessment calendar: which summative tasks fall in the next eight weeks, which criteria each one is assessed against, and what the teacher's feedback on the last one said. Most Dubai schools publish this per subject at the start of a term, and most parents have it in an email they have not opened. Ten minutes finding it changes the whole shape of the first month. The coordinator will send it again if you ask, and the subject teachers hold the detail behind each line of it.

The second thing is the year's own geography. A Dubai school year starts in late summer and runs in three terms, with the UAE weekend on Saturday and Sunday and a short Friday. Ramadan moves earlier each year and sits inside the school calendar, shifting when revision realistically happens. Half-terms are short and are where catch-up either happens or does not. And in the final Middle Years year there is the Personal Project, which has a deadline that will not move and which almost every student starts later than they should.

The rest of this page is written as a calendar. What the next eight weeks have to achieve. Where the year's pressure points sit and what to do before each one. What the four criteria actually reward, in the language the descriptors use. How to plan a Personal Project from its deadline backwards. And what the Middle Years years should be quietly building towards if your child is heading for the Diploma. Teaching is one-to-one over live video; IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE, since home visiting is a service offered only in India.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.description: Four criteria covering knowledge and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts. The criterion that costs marks most often is communication: correct answers presented without the reasoning visible, which the descriptors do not reward however right the answer is.

subjects.name: Sciences
subjects.description: Criteria covering knowing and understanding, inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating, and reflecting on the impacts of science. Students lose most in processing and evaluating, where data is presented but not interpreted, and limitations are listed without being ranked by importance.

subjects.name: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Analysing, organising, producing text and using language. The common gap is analysing: students summarise what a text says rather than examining how the writer achieves an effect, which is a different task and marked differently.

subjects.name: Language Acquisition
subjects.description: Listening, reading, speaking and writing, assessed by phase rather than by year group. Progress depends heavily on production rather than recognition, so a student who understands far more than they can produce will score below what their comprehension suggests.

subjects.name: Individuals and Societies
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, investigating, communicating, and thinking critically. Thinking critically is where marks go: evidence is presented without the source being evaluated, or a conclusion restates the argument rather than weighing it.

subjects.name: Design
subjects.description: Inquiring and analysing, developing ideas, creating the solution, and evaluating. The design cycle is marked as a process, so a strong final product with a thin development section still scores in the middle, which surprises students every year.

subjects.name: Arts
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, developing skills, thinking creatively, and responding. The process journal carries real marks, and students who make good work without documenting its development lose them in the criteria that assess the thinking.

subjects.name: Physical and Health Education
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, planning for performance, applying and performing, and reflecting and improving performance. The written and reflective criteria are the ones that cost marks, often for students who are strong performers and weak documenters.

subjects.name: Interdisciplinary units
subjects.description: Assessed units that deliberately cross two subject groups, with their own criteria covering disciplinary grounding, synthesising and reflecting. Students who treat them as two separate pieces of work rather than one integrated argument lose the synthesis marks.

subjects.name: Personal Project
subjects.description: An independent project with a goal the student sets, assessed on planning, applying skills and reflecting. Marks are lost in the process journal and the report rather than in the product. The work must be the student's own; coaching is about process and criteria literacy only.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-al-mizhar.regionsTitle: The Al Mizhar catchment, and how its calendar varies
dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-al-mizhar.regionsIntro: School calendars in Dubai are not identical, and in a catchment where families use schools in several directions that matters. The notes below say what varies, not what is nearby.

regions.name: Mirdif
regions.note: Where most of the schools this catchment uses sit, including continuum provision. Term dates and assessment weeks here are the ones most Al Mizhar families plan around, and they are published per subject at the start of each term.

regions.name: Al Khawaneej
regions.note: Primary provision and a Dubai Schools campus, with secondary students travelling. Families here often have children in two schools with two different assessment calendars, which is a real scheduling problem rather than a theoretical one.

regions.name: Al Warqa
regions.note: Large cohorts and correspondingly large assessment weeks, where several summative tasks can land in the same fortnight. Knowing that pattern in advance is what makes an eight-week plan realistic rather than optimistic.

regions.name: Al Rashidiya
regions.note: A shorter run towards Deira and the airport corridor. Mainly relevant because journey direction decides whether a student's working evening starts at five or six, which across a Middle Years year is a great many hours.

regions.name: Nad Al Hamar
regions.note: Some families here use schools south of the creek, which can mean a different half-term alignment from their neighbours. Where two schools in one household differ, the tutoring calendar has to follow the child with the nearer deadline.

regions.name: Dubai Silicon Oasis
regions.note: A longer run with growing secondary provision. Evening traffic on the Academic City road is the practical constraint on how early a weekday session can start for families travelling that way.

regions.name: Al Qusais
regions.note: Among the longest routes from this part of Dubai. Students on these runs lose the most usable weekday time, which is why their Personal Project timeline has to start earlier than a Mirdif classmate's.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-al-mizhar.modesIntro: Three ways of running Middle Years support, chosen by where the student sits in the year rather than by preference. All are taught one-to-one over live video to Al Mizhar households.

modes.title: Task-cycle support
modes.description: The default shape. Work is organised around the next summative task: which criteria it is assessed against, what the descriptor at the top band actually asks for, and what the last piece of teacher feedback said was missing. The session before a task looks different from the session after it, deliberately.
bullets: Starts from the school's published assessment calendar
Reads the criterion descriptors with the student, in their own words
Rehearses the task type rather than the topic content
Reviews the returned mark against the descriptor afterwards

modes.title: Criterion repair
modes.description: A short block aimed at one criterion that is consistently costing marks across subjects. Communication in mathematics, processing and evaluating in sciences, and thinking critically in individuals and societies are the usual candidates. Because criteria recur in every unit, fixing one pays back repeatedly for the rest of the year.
bullets: Diagnoses from marked tasks across two or three subjects
Targets the criterion, not the subject
Uses the student's own returned work as the material
Ends when the criterion stops appearing in the loss log

modes.title: Personal Project coaching
modes.description: Process support in the final Middle Years year, planned backwards from the submission date. The coaching covers goal setting that is actually achievable, keeping a process journal that earns marks, and understanding what each criterion rewards. The project, the journal and the report are written by the student throughout.
bullets: Backward plan built from the school's own deadline
Goal narrowed until it is achievable in the time available
Process journal habits established in the first fortnight
Feedback on the student's own drafts; no writing or rewriting

sections.heading: What the next eight weeks actually have to achieve
paragraphs: Eight weeks is the useful planning unit in the Middle Years Programme, because it is roughly the distance between one summative task and the next in most subjects, and it is short enough that a student can see the end of it. Planning a whole year produces a document nobody reads. Planning eight weeks produces work that gets done.

The first move is to find out what is actually coming. Most Dubai schools publish a per-subject assessment outline at the start of a term, naming the summative tasks and the criteria each is assessed against. Lay those out on one page and the picture is usually uncomfortable: three tasks in one fortnight, nothing for three weeks, then two more. That clustering is the thing to plan around, because a student cannot produce their best work on three tasks in nine days if the preparation all happens in those nine days.

The second move is to decide what the eight weeks are for. If a criterion keeps costing marks across subjects, the block should fix the criterion and accept that content coverage will be slightly thinner. If a single subject has collapsed, the block should be about that subject and nothing else. Trying to do both produces a plan with eleven priorities, which is the same as having none. Pick one, write it at the top, and judge the block at the end against that single thing. A block judged against one written aim also tells you something at the end, which a block with eleven aims never does.
bullets: Eight weeks is short enough to finish and long enough to change a grade
Summative tasks cluster; plan around the clusters, not the average week
One priority per block, written down, judged at the end
Content coverage is the thing to sacrifice when a criterion needs fixing

sections.heading: The Middle Years year, laid out backwards
paragraphs: Working a year backwards from its end points is the method competitors in this market do not use, and it is the one that makes a plan feel finite. The table below is the shape of a Dubai Middle Years year, built from what is common across schools in this catchment rather than from any one school's dates. Your own school's calendar overrides every row of it, and the Middle Years coordinator is the person who holds the authoritative version.

A few features of the UAE year are worth naming because they do not appear in international guidance. The weekend is Saturday and Sunday with a short Friday, which makes Saturday morning the most underused productive hour in most households. Ramadan sits inside the academic year and moves earlier annually, shortening school days and shifting the useful working window into the evening. And the long summer break falls across the hottest months, which makes it the natural place for foundation work that term time cannot accommodate.

The row most families underestimate is the one before a reporting window. Marks that go on a report are the marks from tasks already completed, so the work that changes a report has to happen six to eight weeks before it is written, not in the fortnight before parents' evening. That single piece of timing explains most of the frustration families feel about Middle Years reporting, and acting on it is free. Treat the table as a prompt for the conversation with the coordinator rather than as the dates themselves.

sections.heading: Criteria A to D: what the grade is actually made of
paragraphs: Every Middle Years subject group assesses four criteria, each marked out of eight, and the criteria differ by group. This is the single most useful thing a parent can understand about the programme, because it explains the recurring complaint that a child who knows the subject is not getting the marks. Knowing the subject is one criterion. There are three others, and they reward planning, communication and evaluation, which are separate skills that can be taught.

The practical move is to read the descriptors with the student. Not summarise them, read them. The top band of a communication criterion in mathematics says something specific about using appropriate forms of representation and about reasoning being complete and coherent. A student who has read that sentence knows why their correct answer scored four, and a student who has only been told to show their working does not. The descriptors are published by the school, and reading one takes four minutes.

The table sets out which criterion tends to cost marks in each group across this catchment. It is a pattern rather than a rule, and your child's own marked tasks are the real evidence. The reason it is worth having is that criteria recur in every unit of every year, so a criterion fixed in October keeps paying marks in March. Content, by contrast, has to be learned once per unit. That asymmetry is why criterion repair is usually the better use of a tutoring block than another pass through content.

sections.heading: Summative tasks are the grade. Homework usually is not
paragraphs: A recurring source of confusion in Al Mizhar households is a student who does all their homework diligently and receives a middling Middle Years grade. The explanation is structural. Formative work, including most homework, is practice: it informs teaching and it should inform the student, but the grade on the report is built from summative tasks assessed against the criteria. A student who works hard on formative tasks and treats the summative as just another piece of work has misunderstood where the marks live.

This is not an argument for ignoring homework. Formative work is where a misunderstanding should be caught, and it is free diagnostic information that most families throw away. The argument is for a different allocation of effort in the days before a summative task: rehearsing the task type, re-reading the criterion descriptors, and looking at what the teacher said about the last comparable task. That preparation is often the difference between a five and a seven on a criterion, and it takes an hour.

There is a parallel point about feedback. Returned summative tasks carry the most useful information a student will get all term, and they are frequently filed unread. A fifteen-minute routine, reading the teacher's comments, locating the criterion that scored lowest, and writing one sentence about what would have earned the next band, converts each returned task into an improvement. Over a year that is perhaps a dozen such conversions, which is more than any amount of extra content teaching will deliver.
bullets: Report grades come from summative tasks, not from homework volume
Formative work is free diagnostic information most families discard
An hour of task-type rehearsal often outperforms an evening of content
Every returned task should produce one written sentence about the next band

sections.heading: The Personal Project, planned from the deadline backwards
paragraphs: In the final Middle Years year the Personal Project arrives with a fixed submission date and a set of criteria that reward process over product. Almost every student starts late, and almost every late start produces the same result: a reasonable outcome with a thin process journal and a report written in a weekend, which scores in the middle whatever the product looks like. Starting on time is worth more than talent here, and starting on time requires the plan to be built backwards from the date.

The second common failure is a goal that was never achievable. A student who sets out to build something requiring equipment, permissions or six months finds themselves three weeks from submission with nothing to document. Narrowing a goal until it can genuinely be completed, and documented, in the time available is the most valuable hour of coaching in the whole project. It is also an hour students resist, because narrowing feels like giving up on the interesting version.

The boundary here matters and is worth stating in both directions. A coach may help a student test whether a goal is achievable, explain what each criterion rewards, suggest how to keep a process journal that earns marks, and give feedback on drafts the student has written. A coach may not write any part of the report or the journal, rewrite the student's sentences, or produce the product. The project is assessed as the student's own work and submitted as such. Operators selling finished coursework exist in this market; using one puts the student's own standing at risk.

sections.heading: Ramadan, the short Friday and where the hours actually are
paragraphs: A tutoring plan that ignores the UAE calendar fails for ordinary reasons. The weekend falls on Saturday and Sunday and Friday is short, which means the week has a different shape from the one most international guidance assumes. For a Middle Years student in Al Mizhar on a bus route to Mirdif or further, the practical weekday window is narrow: arrival, a break, a meal, and then perhaps ninety minutes of real attention before the evening collapses.

Saturday morning is the hour nobody uses and almost everybody should. A rested student at nine in the morning is a different student from the one who arrives home at five, and tasks that need sustained thought, a mathematics investigation, a piece of analytical writing, a Personal Project drafting session, belong in that slot rather than in a tired weekday hour. Families resist it because the weekend feels like it should be free; the compromise that usually works is one weekend morning hour in exchange for a protected weekday evening.

Ramadan reshapes the month rather than cancelling it. School days shorten, the household rhythm shifts and the useful working window moves into the evening after Iftar. Sessions can simply move there, and a student who keeps a weekly slot through the month arrives at the term afterwards without a four-week hole in their work. The alternative, pausing and resuming, consistently costs more than the month saved, because the restart repeats work that had already been secured.
bullets: The UAE week has a short Friday and a Saturday-Sunday weekend
Saturday morning is the most productive underused hour in most households
Ramadan sessions move after Iftar instead of pausing for a month
Weekday capacity after a long bus route is about ninety real minutes

sections.heading: What the Middle Years years should quietly be building for the Diploma
paragraphs: If your child is heading for the Diploma, the Middle Years years are not just five years to be survived. They are where the habits the Diploma assumes either form or do not. The transition catches students in three specific places, and all three are addressable earlier and much more cheaply than they are in Year 12.

The first is quantitative fluency. Middle Years science is assessed against criteria, and a student can score well while having done comparatively little calculation. Diploma sciences assume rearrangement, unit tracking and uncertainty handling from early in the first term. A Middle Years student who practises those deliberately, even a little, arrives in a different position from one who met them for the first time in the Diploma.

The second is sustained independent writing. The Middle Years offers scaffolding; the Extended Essay does not, and neither does a Diploma internal investigation. A student who has written a Personal Project report properly, from their own planning and their own journal, has done a small version of that work already. The third is time horizon: Middle Years deadlines are weeks away, Diploma deadlines are months away, and a student who has never managed a months-long piece of work will manage their first one badly. The Personal Project is the rehearsal, which is another reason not to leave it until the last term. None of this requires extra hours. It requires the hours already being spent to be pointed at the habits the next programme assumes, which is a question of what the work is rather than how much of it there is.

sections.heading: Starting, and the coverage limit stated before you ask
paragraphs: Send three things and the first session becomes useful immediately: the school's assessment outline for this term, one or two marked summative tasks with the criterion marks and teacher comments intact, and the realistic weekday time your child walks in the door. The first two give the diagnosis, the third decides whether the slot you book is one your child can actually use.

Then a free trial lesson, one-to-one over live video. Ask the tutor to look at the marked tasks and tell you which criterion is costing marks and what the next task needs. A tutor who can answer that inside the hour has read the descriptors and understands the programme. A tutor who talks about the Middle Years in general terms has not. If the match is wrong, say so in week one; it costs nothing then and costs a term later.

The limit, said plainly: Middle Years coverage is by subject group, and some groups are thinly staffed in the UAE, particularly language acquisition in less common languages and specific arts strands. Where no UAE-based specialist has a slot that fits an Al Mizhar schedule, you will be told, and offered a specialist based elsewhere teaching over the same live video on Gulf Standard Time. Nothing is substituted quietly. No competitor page reviewed for this project discloses a coverage limit at all, which is why this one does. Everything else, the slot, the subject group, the length of the first block, is decided in that first conversation and can be changed afterwards.

process.title: Send the assessment calendar
process.description: The school's per-subject outline for this term, naming the summative tasks and the criteria each is assessed against. This is the document that makes a plan specific, and most parents already have it in an unopened email from the first week of term.

process.title: Send two marked summative tasks
process.description: With criterion marks and teacher comments left on. Two tasks from different subjects are better than two from one, because they show whether the problem is a subject or a criterion. That distinction decides what the first eight weeks are for.

process.title: Pick one priority for eight weeks
process.description: A criterion, or a subject, not both. Write it down. Eight weeks is long enough to move a criterion and short enough that a student can see the end of it, and a block with one stated aim can actually be judged at the end.

process.title: Free trial as a diagnostic
process.description: One hour over live video with the marked tasks read in advance. Ask which criterion is costing marks and what the next task needs. You should finish knowing the answer to both, and what the first block will do about it.

process.title: Review against the next returned task
process.description: Not against how the sessions felt. Did the criterion mark move? If it did, continue. If it did not after three or four sessions, the method changes rather than the hours increasing.

whyPoints.title: Planned from the calendar, not the textbook
whyPoints.description: Middle Years grades come from dated summative tasks, so the plan starts from the school's assessment outline. Working generically through a subject produces a student who knows more and scores the same, because the criterion costing marks was never addressed.

whyPoints.title: Criterion descriptors read, not summarised
whyPoints.description: Sessions read the actual top-band descriptor with the student. A child who has read what a communication criterion asks for understands why a correct answer scored four; a child told to show their working does not.

whyPoints.title: Leverage from criteria over content
whyPoints.description: Criteria recur in every unit of every year, so one fixed in October keeps paying marks in March. Content has to be learned once per unit. That asymmetry is why criterion repair usually beats another content pass.

whyPoints.title: The Personal Project started on time
whyPoints.description: Coaching builds the plan backwards from the school's own deadline and narrows the goal until it is achievable. Starting on time is worth more than talent on this project, and the process criteria are where the marks actually sit.

whyPoints.title: Written on the coursework boundary
whyPoints.description: A coach tests feasibility, explains criteria and gives feedback on the student's own drafts. A coach does not write, rewrite or produce the work. Operators selling finished coursework are active in this market, and this page states the boundary rather than implying it.

whyPoints.title: Built around the UAE week
whyPoints.description: Short Friday, Saturday and Sunday weekend, Ramadan timings and a ninety-minute weekday window after a long bus route. Plans that ignore these fail for ordinary reasons rather than academic ones.

faqs.question: Why does my child do all the homework and still get a middling MYP grade?
faqs.answer: Because the report grade is built from summative tasks assessed against the four criteria, and most homework is formative practice rather than assessed work. A student who works hard on formative tasks and treats a summative as just another piece of work has misunderstood where the marks sit. The fix is cheap: in the days before a summative, rehearse the task type, re-read the criterion descriptors and look at what the teacher said about the last comparable task. That hour frequently moves a criterion by a band.

faqs.question: What do the four MYP criteria actually assess?
faqs.answer: Four criteria per subject group, each marked out of eight, and they differ between groups. Knowing the subject is only one of them; the others reward planning, communication and evaluation, which are separate teachable skills. In sciences they cover knowing and understanding, inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating, and reflecting on impacts. In mathematics they cover knowledge, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts. Your school publishes the descriptors, and reading one takes four minutes.

faqs.question: Which criterion should an Al Mizhar family look at first on a marked task?
faqs.answer: It varies by subject group, but a pattern shows up repeatedly. Communicating in mathematics, where correct answers arrive with the reasoning invisible. Processing and evaluating in sciences, where data is presented but not interpreted and limitations are listed without being ranked. Analysing in language and literature, where a student summarises what a text says instead of examining how an effect is achieved. Thinking critically in individuals and societies, where evidence appears without the source being weighed. Your child's own marked tasks are the real evidence.

faqs.question: How far ahead should we plan MYP support for a student in Al Mizhar?
faqs.answer: Eight weeks, as a working unit. It is roughly the distance between summative tasks in most subjects and short enough that a student can see the end of it. Planning a whole year produces a document nobody reads. The first step is laying this term's assessment outlines on one page, which usually reveals that tasks cluster: three in a fortnight, then nothing for three weeks. Preparation has to happen before a cluster rather than inside it, and that single piece of timing is most of the plan.

faqs.question: When should a Personal Project actually start?
faqs.answer: Earlier than almost anyone does, and the plan should be built backwards from the school's submission date rather than forwards from enthusiasm. The criteria reward process, so a thin process journal caps the mark however good the product is. The two decisions that matter happen at the start: narrowing the goal until it is genuinely achievable and documentable in the time available, and establishing a weekly journal habit. A journal written retrospectively in the final weeks reads exactly like one, and is marked accordingly.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with the Personal Project without doing it for my child?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the boundary is worth stating both ways. A coach may test whether a goal is achievable with the time, access and skills available, explain what each criterion rewards, suggest how to keep a process journal that earns marks, and give feedback on drafts the student has written. A coach may not write any part of the report or journal, rewrite the student's sentences, or produce the product. The project is assessed and submitted as the student's own work, and operators selling finished coursework put that at risk.

faqs.question: Does the MYP prepare a student properly for the IB Diploma?
faqs.answer: It prepares them well for inquiry and criterion-referenced work, and less well for three specific things. Quantitative fluency, because Middle Years science can be scored well with comparatively little calculation while Diploma sciences assume rearrangement and uncertainty handling early. Sustained independent writing without scaffolding. And managing a piece of work with a months-long horizon rather than a weeks-long one. All three are addressable during the Middle Years years far more cheaply than in Year 12, and the Personal Project is the rehearsal for the last two.

faqs.question: Does my child's school enter students for formal MYP assessment at the end?
faqs.answer: That is a school-level decision and you need to ask. Some schools enter candidates for on-screen examinations and ePortfolios leading to a Middle Years certificate, and others complete the programme without external assessment. It changes the shape of the final year substantially, including how much practice under timed conditions is appropriate. The Middle Years coordinator holds the answer and can give it in a sentence. Any tutoring plan for the final year should be built on their answer rather than on an assumption.

faqs.question: How do Ramadan timings affect a tutoring schedule in Dubai?
faqs.answer: School days shorten and the household rhythm moves later, so the useful working window shifts into the evening after Iftar. Sessions move there rather than stopping, and a student who keeps a weekly slot through the month arrives at the following term without a four-week hole. Pausing and resuming consistently costs more than the month saved, because the restart repeats work that had already been secured. Confirm your own school's published Ramadan timings, since they vary between schools in this catchment.

faqs.question: My child is strong in class discussion and weak on written tasks. What is that?
faqs.answer: Usually a criterion problem rather than a knowledge problem, and it is one of the most common patterns in the Middle Years. A student who reasons well aloud but writes thinly is losing communication and analysis marks, not understanding marks. The work is specific: taking a point the student just made verbally and writing it in the form the descriptor asks for, repeatedly, until the written version carries the same content as the spoken one. It responds quickly once it is named, and it is invisible if nobody looks at the criterion marks.

faqs.question: Is it worth tutoring a Year 7 or Year 8 MYP student at all?
faqs.answer: Often yes, and for a different reason than parents expect. The early Middle Years years are when criterion literacy forms: understanding what a descriptor asks for, keeping a process record, writing reasoning rather than answers. A student who builds those habits at eleven or twelve carries them through five years and into the Diploma. Tutoring at this stage should be light and habit-focused rather than content-heavy. If the enquiry is really about a content gap, that is also worth addressing, but it is usually narrower than it feels.

faqs.question: How many sessions a week does an Al Mizhar MYP student need?
faqs.answer: One, in most cases, placed well. The Middle Years workload is spread across eight subject groups, so adding a second weekly session for one subject often just displaces work in another. The exception is a task cluster or a Personal Project deadline, where a short burst of two sessions a week for a fortnight makes sense and then stops. For a student on a long bus route, the binding constraint is attention rather than available hours, which is why a weekend morning usually outperforms a second weekday evening.

faqs.question: What should we do with a returned summative task?
faqs.answer: Spend fifteen minutes on it rather than filing it. Read the teacher's comments, find the criterion that scored lowest, and write one sentence describing what would have earned the next band. That is the whole routine. Done across a year it converts perhaps a dozen returned tasks into a dozen specific improvements, which is more movement than an equivalent amount of extra content teaching produces. Returned work carries the most useful information a student gets all term, and most of it is thrown away unread.

faqs.question: What should an Al Mizhar family send before a first MYP session?
faqs.answer: Three things. The school's assessment outline for this term, naming the summative tasks and their criteria. One or two marked summative tasks from different subjects, with criterion marks and teacher comments intact. And the realistic weekday time your child walks in the door after the bus. The first two produce the diagnosis, including whether the problem is a subject or a criterion. The third decides whether the slot you book is one your child can actually work in rather than one that looks tidy on a calendar.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-al-mizhar.closingBody: Middle Years marks come from dated tasks assessed on four criteria, which makes the school's assessment outline the most useful document in the house. Lay this term's tasks on one page, find the criterion that keeps costing marks, and give the next eight weeks one stated job. Send two marked summative tasks and take a free trial lesson as a diagnostic: a tutor who can name the criterion inside the hour has read the descriptors. Lessons run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, and move after Iftar during Ramadan rather than stopping.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-al-muteena.tutorsIntro: The tutors here work to a dated plan rather than an open arrangement: a named subject group, a named criterion, a block with an end date and a target. Each works from the student's own task calendar and the school's published descriptors.

intro.heading: Why MYP support almost always starts three weeks late
paragraphs: The sequence is remarkably consistent. A student submits a unit task in week four of term. It is marked in week six. It appears on a report in week eight. The parent reads the report in week nine, discusses it at a parents' evening in week ten, and starts looking for a tutor in week eleven. By the time a first session happens, the unit is finished, the next unit is half taught, and the criterion that produced the low mark will not be assessed again for a month.

That lag is why MYP tutoring so often feels like it achieves nothing. The work is not wrong; the timing is. Criterion-based assessment gives a student repeated chances at the same criterion across a year, but only if the intervention arrives before the next assessed task rather than after the last one. A plan anchored to the task calendar rather than to the reporting calendar changes what the same number of sessions can do.

Getting ahead of it requires information the school already publishes and families rarely collect. Most Dubai MYP schools issue a unit overview or assessment calendar per subject group, showing which units run when and which criteria each task assesses. With those in hand, a parent can see that the Sciences task in week six assesses inquiring and designing, which means the week-four session should be about designing a controlled investigation rather than about last term's low mark.

The calendar also explains why some terms are impossible. A Dubai MYP student carries eight subject groups plus the Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies that KHDA requires of every private school regardless of curriculum. Assessed tasks do not arrive evenly: they cluster at the end of units, which means three or four land in the same fortnight twice a term. A tutoring plan that assumes a steady weekly load will be overwhelmed in those fortnights and underused between them.

And in MYP 5 there is a second calendar running underneath the first. The Personal Project has its own sequence of checkpoints spread across most of the year, each one a school deadline rather than an IB one, and it is the piece of work with no weekly lesson to keep it moving. It is therefore the thing that slips, every year, in every school, and it slips invisibly until a checkpoint is missed.

What follows is that calendar laid out: the Dubai MYP year term by term, the Personal Project counted backwards, what an eight-week block can and cannot achieve, how Ramadan sits inside it, and what a term of support costs when it is budgeted by term rather than by hour. None of it requires more hours than a family was already prepared to buy; it requires the same hours placed differently in the year, which costs nothing extra and is the one change most households never make.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-al-muteena.programmesIntro: The calendar differs by stage, so it is worth being clear which part of the programme a family is planning around.

programmes.name: Early Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four criteria each, with units running six to ten weeks and an assessed task at the end of most of them. Marks at this stage are formative in practice even where they are reported, which makes these the cheapest years in which to fix a habit such as never naming a control variable.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai schools report two or three times a year at this stage, so the lag between work and parental sight of it is longest here. Families in Al Muteena whose children are in MYP 2 or 3 have the most room to work on process and the least urgency pressing them, which is the usual reason nothing happens until MYP 4.

programmes.name: MYP 4 and MYP 5
programmes.description: The years where marks begin to matter for school progression and for Diploma or IGCSE placement. Task volume rises, interdisciplinary units appear, and MYP 5 adds the Personal Project. Students who have never been taught to read a criterion descriptor meet the consequences here rather than earlier.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai this is also when the next-stage decision is made, and the local school mix matters: most schools near Al Muteena run IGCSE rather than Diploma, so a MYP 5 student here is often choosing between staying in the IB system at a school further south or moving to a nearby IGCSE and A Level route.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: The destination that reshapes how MYP 5 should be spent. Diploma assessment is external and timed, graded 1 to 7 on papers plus internal assessment, with the core adding points. A student arriving from MYP has strong process habits and little experience of writing a complete argument against a clock.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai's 2026-27 intake adds seven new private schools including three International Baccalaureate, creating around sixteen thousand eight hundred new places. For an MYP 4 student in the northern districts that widens the Diploma options available by the time the decision has to be made.

programmes.name: IGCSE as the alternative at the end of MYP
programmes.description: The route many Dubai students switch into, usually at the end of Year 9. Externally examined with public past papers and tiering in several subjects, which is a different assessment culture rather than a harder or easier one. The switch costs a term of adjustment in technique more than in content.
programmes.countryNote: UAE candidates sit Cambridge IGCSE in the June and November series; the February/March series is offered to India only. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs May/June and November, with its November 2026 final timetable running from late October to 19 November 2026 and November 2025 results reaching students on 22 January 2026.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-al-muteena.subjectsIntro: Below are the MYP subject groups described by when their assessed tasks tend to land and what the task usually asks for, because that is the information a dated plan needs.

subjects.name: MYP Sciences
subjects.description: Investigation tasks cluster at unit endings and almost always assess inquiring and designing alongside processing and evaluating. The design work has to be taught before the task, not after it, because a flawed method cannot be analysed well however good the write-up is.

subjects.name: MYP Mathematics
subjects.description: Tests assessing knowing and understanding arrive regularly; investigation tasks assessing patterns and justification arrive once or twice a term. The second kind is where grades move, and it needs preparation several weeks ahead of the date.

subjects.name: MYP Language and Literature
subjects.description: Assessed writing and oral tasks spread more evenly than in other groups, which makes this the subject where weekly work compounds best. Precision of textual evidence is the recurring gap rather than fluency.

subjects.name: MYP Individuals and Societies
subjects.description: Research-based investigations land at unit ends and need a focused question agreed early. The thinking critically criterion rewards weighed evidence, so the research has to be planned to produce more than one perspective.

subjects.name: MYP Design
subjects.description: The design cycle runs across a whole unit, so the folder is being assessed continuously rather than at one deadline. Students who build first and document last lose marks that were available throughout, and the fix has to start at the beginning of the unit.

subjects.name: MYP Language Acquisition
subjects.description: Assessed across listening, reading, speaking and writing on a rotating basis, so a weak strand can go a term without being assessed and then dominate a report. Checking which strand is next is the useful question.

subjects.name: MYP Arts and Physical and Health Education
subjects.description: Both carry written criteria the practical work does not satisfy: process journals in the arts, written plans and reflections in physical education. These are the easiest marks in the programme to recover and the most often left.

subjects.name: Interdisciplinary units
subjects.description: Scheduled once or twice a year and assessed on their own criteria. Because they sit outside the normal subject rhythm, they are frequently treated as extra homework and lose the synthesis marks that are the entire point.

subjects.name: The Personal Project
subjects.description: Runs across most of the final year with school checkpoints rather than lessons. It has no weekly pressure, which is precisely why it slips, and the process journal is the part that suffers first and costs most.

regions.name: Al Muteena
regions.note: Apartment living with shared study space, so the useful commitment is a fixed hour the household protects rather than a particular time of day. Little IB provision nearby means the school is almost always a bus ride south.

regions.name: Hor Al Anz
regions.note: On the same school routes, which means the same unit calendars and the same assessment weeks. Two students from these districts at the same school will have identical task clusters, which is worth knowing when planning blocks.

regions.name: Deira
regions.note: Large school stock weighted to IGCSE and Indian curricula, so MYP students here are a small minority locally and term dates vary between neighbours' schools more than families expect.

regions.name: Al Qusais
regions.note: Mixed curricula with different term calendars in the same street. A family with children on two systems is managing two sets of assessment weeks, which is the practical case for planning by date rather than by habit.

regions.name: Al Garhoud
regions.note: The closest concentration of IB provision. Students resident here get home earliest, which makes weekday sessions viable in the weeks when three tasks land together.

regions.name: Oud Metha and Bur Dubai
regions.note: Further IB schools with a longer journey north. Arrival after five means that in heavy assessment weeks the realistic extra hour is a weekend morning rather than another weekday evening.

sections.heading: What eight weeks of MYP support can and cannot achieve
paragraphs: Eight weeks is roughly one unit plus its assessed task, which makes it the natural unit of planning in the Middle Years Programme. Within that window a criterion that fails on a documented behaviour can realistically move. Naming independent, dependent and controlled variables. Structuring a method another person could follow. Quoting precisely rather than at length. Writing a reflection that analyses rather than apologises. These are things a student can start doing in the next task, and the mark responds immediately because the descriptor is describing a behaviour rather than a body of knowledge.

Within the same eight weeks a criterion that fails on knowing and understanding usually does not move far, because content has to be taught and then used, and the assessed tasks in one unit cover one unit's content. A student two years behind in mathematical fluency will not be caught up in eight weeks by anyone, and a provider implying otherwise is selling rather than teaching.

That distinction decides what to buy. If the criterion breakdown shows a weak inquiring and designing in Sciences, or a weak reflection across several subjects, an eight-week block aimed at exactly that is a good purchase with a measurable outcome. If the breakdown shows a flat profile of low marks across all four criteria in several subjects, the honest answer is a longer plan with content teaching at its centre, and saying so at the start avoids a disappointed review in week eight.

What makes the block work is the end date. An arrangement with no end is never evaluated, because stopping requires a decision and continuing does not. A block that expires forces the family and the tutor to look at the resulting task mark and say plainly whether it moved. That is uncomfortable occasionally and useful always, and it is the main reason this page recommends it over an open weekly commitment.

sections.heading: The Dubai MYP year, term by term
paragraphs: A standard Dubai school year runs in three terms from late August or early September to late June or early July, with a long winter break in December, a shorter spring break, and the summer gap. Within that, MYP units run six to ten weeks each, which means most subject groups set two assessed tasks per term. The practical consequence is that each term contains two task clusters rather than a steady drip, and those clusters are when the student is under genuine pressure.

Term one is the cheapest term to intervene in and the term when nobody does, because the first report has not arrived. A student who starts the year having never read a criterion descriptor will produce two terms of mid-band work before anyone acts. Reading the descriptors for the four criteria in the two weakest subjects, in week two of term one, costs an hour and changes a year.

Term two carries the heaviest load in most Dubai schools: the longest teaching stretch, mid-year reporting, and in MYP 5 the Personal Project's middle checkpoints, where projects either gain momentum or stall quietly. It is also the term Ramadan usually touches in the current cycle, which compresses the school day and moves family routines.

Term three is short, assessment-dense and too late for most things. End-of-year tasks, final reports, and for MYP 5 the completion of the Personal Project and the handover to the next programme. Support purchased in term three is mostly damage limitation on tasks already in flight, which is a legitimate purchase and a much less efficient one than the same money spent in term one.

sections.heading: The Personal Project counted backwards from submission
paragraphs: The Personal Project is the only substantial piece of MYP work with no weekly lesson attached, and that single fact explains almost every problem families have with it. Nothing external pushes it forward between checkpoints, the checkpoints are months apart, and a student who is busy with eight subject groups will deprioritise the thing nobody is chasing. The result is a product built in a fortnight and a process journal reconstructed from memory, which caps the grade regardless of how good the product is.

Counting backwards from the school's submission date produces the plan. Before submission comes the report and the final journal entries. Before that, the product completed with time to reflect on it rather than in a rush. Before that, a halfway review where most projects need redirecting. Before that, a documented plan with a goal specific enough to be assessed. And at the start, a goal chosen for being achievable and assessable rather than impressive.

The journal is where the marks live and where students put the least effort. The criteria reward documented planning, applied skills and genuine reflection, which means entries written while the work is happening, including the entries about things that went wrong. A journal that records a dead end and the decision taken afterwards is better evidence than one recording a smooth path that did not happen.

The boundary for a tutor is absolute and worth repeating. A tutor can help the student set an assessable goal, plan backwards from the checkpoints, read the criteria together, ask hard questions at the halfway point and give feedback on the student's own entries. A tutor cannot write the journal, draft the report, make the product or edit the writing to completion. Operations selling completed assessed work exist in this market, and the consequences of using one land on the student.

sections.heading: Ramadan, the UAE subjects, and the hours that actually exist
paragraphs: A plan that ignores the UAE calendar fails in predictable places. KHDA requires Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, with its requirements to be implemented from the start of the 2025-26 academic year. Those subjects take real timetable hours and generate their own homework, on top of eight MYP subject groups.

KHDA also prescribes how they are organised, which affects a student's week more than families realise. Schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ. Standard Arabic is required as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arab students and for Arabic as a first language. Instructional time is calculated on a forty-minute lesson unit, with KHDA advising at least twenty-five minutes for any mandatory-subject lesson.

Ramadan compresses the school day and reshapes the household evening. In the older northern districts that usually means tutoring moves to after Iftar or to weekend mornings for the month, which online delivery makes a calendar change rather than a renegotiation with a driver. The thing to decide in advance is which work pauses: in practice the weekly criterion block can continue in a shorter form, while the Personal Project almost always stalls unless a checkpoint is deliberately placed before the month begins.

The summer gap is the other calendar feature worth planning. A long break between MYP years is enough for fluency in mathematics and a second language to slip measurably, and it is also the only stretch in the year with genuinely free time. A short block of two or three sessions a week in the final weeks of summer, aimed at the content the next year assumes, is the least disruptive support available and the most commonly skipped.

sections.heading: Reports, descriptors and the data a parent can actually get
paragraphs: A Dubai MYP report gives a grade from 1 to 7 per subject group and usually a comment. That is the least useful form the information comes in, because the grade is a conversion of four criterion marks out of eight each, and the four are almost never equal. A 5 can be built from three strong criteria and one weak one, which is a narrow and fixable problem, or from four mid-band marks, which is a broad one. The report does not distinguish them; the portal usually does.

Most schools publish the strand-level marks on their reporting platform, and will provide the unit overview showing which criteria each upcoming task assesses. Those two documents together are what a dated plan is built from. A parent who collects them once at the start of a term has the whole year's intervention points visible, instead of discovering them a fortnight after each one has passed.

There is also a conversation worth having with the subject teacher rather than the tutor, which is what the next task assesses and what the band above the student's current mark actually requires. Teachers answer that question willingly and specifically when asked directly, and the answer is more valuable than a general request for feedback on how the student is doing.

What this adds up to is a shift in what the parent brings. Arriving at a first tutoring session with a report produces a general conversation. Arriving with the strand-level breakdown, the unit calendar and the date of the next assessed task produces a plan with a target and an end date, which is the difference between buying hours and buying an outcome.

sections.heading: Budgeting MYP tutoring by term rather than by hour
paragraphs: Hourly rates make tutoring look like a variable cost when for most families it is a fixed one. Budgeting by term is more honest. An eight-week block at one session a week is eight sessions, and at published Dubai market rates the arithmetic is straightforward. Bestimate's estimates for weekly one-hour sessions run roughly AED 240 to 600 a month at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-band, and AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more for specialist exam-year support, which puts an eight-week block somewhere between a few hundred and a few thousand dirhams depending on the band chosen.

The published hourly bands behind those estimates are worth knowing. Tutopiya advertises from around AED 33 to 52 an hour and EdFlik from AED 45 to 65. Unitors publishes IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. TutorChase lists around AED 270, Bestimate's specialist band runs AED 200 to 450 and above, and BartyED charges AED 650 for premium named tutors. In-home one-to-one visits are published at AED 180 to 500 an hour with travel included, and monthly in-home packages at AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour sessions against roughly AED 799 for eight online sessions. These are the providers' own figures.

For MYP specifically the band matters less than the criterion fluency, and that is not perfectly correlated with price. A mid-band tutor who has taught MYP Sciences and can quote the inquiring and designing descriptors is worth more than a specialist-priced tutor who has only taught Diploma. The question to ask is about MYP experience directly, not about seniority.

A term-based budget also makes the review honest. Three blocks a year across two subjects is a known annual figure that a family can decide on once. An open weekly arrangement that drifts across two years is a larger figure nobody ever decided on, and it is the shape that produces the complaint that tutoring never achieved anything.

sections.heading: Timing the transition out of MYP
paragraphs: The last calendar question in the Middle Years Programme is when to start preparing for what comes after it. The answer is earlier than most families expect and for a narrower purpose than they assume. MYP builds inquiry, documented process and reflection well. It does not build timed written examination technique, because almost nothing in the programme is a timed written examination, and both the Diploma and IGCSE are built on them.

The gaps are specific and consistent: writing to a clock, where an unfinished good answer scores less than a completed adequate one; command-term discipline, where state, explain, evaluate and discuss carry different expectations that MYP descriptors never drill; recall without open resources; and answering the question asked rather than the one prepared for. None of that requires new content, which is why it responds quickly to a short block.

The right time for that block is the final term of MYP 5, after the Personal Project is submitted and before the summer. Six to eight sessions of timed writing under examination conditions, marked honestly, removes most of the first-term shock at the next school. Done in September of Year 12 instead, the same work happens while the student is also meeting a new school, a new programme and a new workload.

For a student switching to IGCSE rather than Diploma the block looks slightly different: past papers, mark schemes and tier awareness rather than extended argument. Either way the trigger is the same date, the end of MYP 5, and either way the cost is a handful of sessions against a term of avoidable difficulty.

sections.heading: Why online delivery is what makes a dated plan possible
paragraphs: Everything on this page depends on sessions moving when the calendar moves. Assessed tasks cluster, so some weeks need two sessions and some need none. Ramadan shifts the evening. A Personal Project checkpoint lands on a Thursday and the useful session is Wednesday. A full timed paper needs a weekend morning. An arrangement that cannot flex to that is an arrangement that will be out of step with the thing it is meant to support.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE. Home tutoring is a service we run only in India, and no tutor will arrive at an address in Al Muteena or anywhere else in the Emirates. All UAE lessons are one-to-one and live over video on Gulf Standard Time, which is what makes a session movable at a day's notice rather than a journey to be renegotiated.

The published in-home market in Dubai is AED 180 to 500 an hour with travel included, against AED 150 to 300 for comparable online work. For a calendar-led plan the travel cost is not only money: a tutor crossing the city can offer one window per evening, and a session lost to a late school bus in an assessment week is the session that mattered most. Across a year that is the difference between a plan that ran and a plan that was repeatedly rearranged.

The honest limitation is unchanged by any of this. A younger MYP student working alone at a screen needs shorter sessions, written follow-ups and a parent who reads the notes, and a student who will not work without someone in the room is not fixed by the format. For families in that position a nearby structured option may be the better call, and the calendar discipline described here applies either way.
