sections.heading: What an MYP tutor actually does, and why it is not subject tutoring
paragraphs: An MYP tutor spends the first session reading rather than teaching. The material is the student's last three marked tasks and the criterion marks attached to them. In almost every case a pattern appears immediately: consistently strong on criterion A, consistently weak on criterion B or D, across every unit for two years. That is not a content problem and it will not be solved by covering the topic again, which is what a general subject tutor will do because it is the only tool they have.

The criteria reward specific behaviours and they are published in plain language. Criterion B in mathematics asks a student to investigate a pattern and justify a general rule. Criterion D in sciences asks for evaluation of the impact of science, not description of it. Criterion A in language and literature asks for analysis of effect, not identification of a device. A student who has never had the descriptor read to them is guessing at what is wanted, and guessing well in two of the four.

So the work is diagnostic first and then narrow. The tutor and student take one piece of the student's own work, read the descriptor for the weak criterion, and mark the work against it together. Then the student rewrites that section and marks it again. After six or eight repetitions the student can predict their criterion mark before the teacher returns it, and at that point the tutoring has done its job. This is a short intervention with a visible end, not an open-ended arrangement, and a tutor who presents it as a two-year commitment is selling something else.

sections.heading: Business Bay against the districts next door, and why the answer does not change
paragraphs: Parents here compare districts because property and school decisions are made together, and it is reasonable to ask whether another address would make support easier to find. On this question the comparison is unusually clean. The MYP criteria are set by the IB and are word for word identical in every school in the table below. A tutor who can read criterion D in sciences can read it for a student in Meydan, Sobha Hartland or Downtown with no adjustment whatever.

What the table actually compares, therefore, is logistics. Which MYP schools each district reaches, how long the afternoon return takes in term time, and the earliest hour a weeknight session can realistically start. Districts with a campus inside them buy an hour of evening, which is worth having. They do not buy access to a subject specialist, because that person is not resident in any of these districts in the first place.

The second thing worth reading from the table is the regulator column. Every district listed sits under the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, which oversees the quality of private education in Dubai and inspects schools annually. An inspection band tells you something real about a school. It tells you nothing about whether a tutor who understands criterion B in MYP mathematics lives nearby, and parents routinely read it as though it did. Commute figures here are term-time observations rather than published data and shift with routing.

One caveat that does favour a particular address: a child who walks to school keeps a predictable evening, and predictability is worth more than an early start. A family in Meydan whose bus time swings by half an hour each day will find a fixed weeknight slot harder to hold than a Business Bay family on a consistent route, and that is a real reason to book the later of two candidate slots.

sections.heading: Eight subject groups, four criteria each, and the one that hurts
paragraphs: The programme has eight subject groups and each is assessed against four criteria lettered A to D, every one marked out of eight. That gives a maximum of 32 criterion marks per subject per reporting cycle. The letters mean different things in different subjects, which is the detail that catches families out: criterion C is communicating in mathematics, processing and evaluating in sciences, and producing text in language and literature.

The table below sets out the criteria by subject group alongside the one that most commonly costs marks. The pattern across cohorts is consistent. The criteria rewarding recall and organisation are the ones students do well. The criteria rewarding investigation, evaluation and critical thinking are the ones they do not, because those are taught as classroom habits rather than as content and a student can go years without anyone showing them what the descriptor actually asks for.

A parent can use this table immediately. Take the last report, find the subject with the lowest criterion mark, read across to see what that criterion rewards, then ask the teacher one question: what would an 7 or 8 on this criterion look like in my child's next task? That question gets a specific answer from almost every MYP teacher, and it is a better starting point than any amount of general revision. Confirm the exact criterion names and strands for your child's year with the school, since the IB revises subject guides periodically.

sections.heading: How criterion marks become the grade on the report
paragraphs: The four criterion marks are added to a total out of 32, and that total is converted to a grade from 1 to 7 using boundaries the IB publishes and schools apply. The conversion is where information is lost, and it is why two children with the same grade can need entirely different help. A student on 19 and a student on 23 both appear as a 5. One is a mark from a 4 and the other is a mark from a 6, and the report does not say which.

The practical consequence for a Business Bay parent is that the converted grade is the least useful number on the page. Ask for the criterion marks, every reporting cycle, in every subject. Most schools provide them as standard and almost all will provide them on request. With those four numbers you can see whether a 5 is improving or sliding, and which single criterion would move the grade if it gained two marks.

This also explains the familiar frustration of a child who works hard and whose grade will not move. If the weak criterion stays weak, the total cannot cross the boundary no matter how much the strong criteria improve, because each criterion is capped at eight. A student scoring 8, 4, 8, 4 is working at the ceiling in half the subject and cannot reach a 7 without addressing the other half. That is a targeted problem with a short solution, and it is invisible from the grade alone. Confirm the boundaries your school applies, as these are the generally published bands rather than a school-specific table.

sections.heading: Where MYP marks actually go missing
paragraphs: Three failures account for most of it. The first is answering the task rather than the criterion. A student writes a good piece of work about the topic and never does the thing the descriptor asks for — justifies nothing, evaluates nothing, compares nothing. The work is not wrong; it is answering a different question. This is the single commonest cause of a capped criterion and it is fixed by reading the descriptor before writing, every time, until it becomes automatic.

The second is the process journal and the documentation. In Design, Arts and the Personal Project the marks sit in the record of what the student did and why, not in the finished artefact. Students who make something impressive and document it thinly score below students who make something modest and document it carefully. Parents find this counterintuitive and it is worth accepting early, because it turns a vague instruction into a concrete weekly habit.

The third is command terms. MYP command terms have fixed meanings and they are the same words the Diploma will use later with the same meanings. Describe, explain, evaluate, justify and analyse want different things and a student who treats them as synonyms loses marks in every subject simultaneously. Fixing command terms once in MYP 3 or 4 pays across eight subject groups and keeps paying for the next five years.

A fourth, smaller leak is worth naming: work handed in without the task sheet beside it. Most MYP tasks are issued with the criteria being assessed printed at the top, and students who never look at that line are guessing at which two of the four matter for this piece. Checking it takes ten seconds and recovers marks on every task.

sections.heading: The Personal Project, and exactly where a tutor stops
paragraphs: In MYP 5 every student completes the Personal Project: a self-directed piece of work with a product or outcome, a process journal and a report, assessed against three criteria — planning, applying skills, and reflecting — for a total of 24 marks. The product is not what is marked. The planning, the evidence of skills applied, and the quality of reflection are. Students who grasp that in the first fortnight routinely outscore students with far more impressive products.

A tutor can be genuinely useful here and the boundary is absolute. The tutor may ask whether a goal is specific enough to be evidenced, whether a success criterion is measurable, whether the journal actually records decisions rather than activities, and whether a reflection is reflecting or just narrating. The tutor may give feedback on a draft the student has written. The tutor may not choose the goal, write the report, draft the reflection, or produce any part of the product.

This matters beyond the marks. Under IB academic-honesty rules, submitting work that is not the student's own is malpractice, and the consequence falls on the student. There are providers in this market selling completed assessed work at four-figure prices; buying it exposes a child to an academic-honesty investigation at the start of their senior school career. Ask any provider to state the no-writing boundary in writing before the Personal Project term begins. A provider who hesitates has answered the question.

Timing helps too. Most of the mark is decided in the first month, when the goal and the success criteria are set, long before the product exists. Two sessions in that first month are worth more than six in the last, and families who book late usually find the tutor can only tidy a reflection that was always going to score what it scores.

sections.heading: MYP 5 into DP1 or into Year 10, and the September gap
paragraphs: The useful question in MYP 5 is not how to raise this year's grades but which gap is coming. A student continuing into the Diploma has been assessed against criteria for five years and will meet timed, externally marked written papers for the first time. The content is usually fine. What is missing is examination behaviour: working to the clock, reading a mark allocation and budgeting words to it, and recognising that a correct answer to the wrong command term earns nothing.

A student transferring into a British school for IGCSE at Year 10 has a different gap. IGCSE rewards content coverage and tiered paper technique, and assumes a body of specific knowledge that the MYP taught through inquiry rather than in syllabus order. Here the summer work is content mapping — finding what the new syllabus assumes and the MYP did not cover in that form — plus tier-appropriate past papers early enough to influence the school's tier decision.

The third route, less common in this corridor, is International A Levels after MYP 5 via a one-year bridge or a direct entry where the school permits it. Whichever route applies, decide it before the summer and plan around that gap specifically. A generic summer tutoring block spends six weeks on content the new school will teach anyway, while the actual difficulty — timed written work for the Diploma, syllabus coverage for IGCSE — goes untouched until October.

Ask both the current school and the receiving one a single question in writing: what do you assume a student knows on day one? The answers are usually specific and they differ, and the difference between them is the summer's work. That one email replaces most of the guessing that otherwise goes into a transition block.

sections.heading: What MYP support costs in this corridor
paragraphs: MYP tutoring tends to be bought in short blocks rather than by the year, which changes how the rates should be read. A criterion-repair block of six to eight sessions is the commonest purchase in this corridor, so the relevant question is what that block costs rather than what an hour costs. At the specialist end of the Dubai market the block lands between roughly AED 1,200 and AED 3,000 depending on the rate; at the generalist end, between about AED 300 and AED 500.

The published hourly figures behind that: Tutopiya advertises from AED 33 to 52 an hour and EdFlik from AED 45 to 65, which is the university-student and generalist band. Unitors publishes IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200 for a qualified subject tutor online. Named IB and IGCSE specialists run roughly AED 200 to 450 and above, with TutorChase at AED 270 and Bestimate's 2026 Dubai table giving 200 to 450 or more. In-home visits including travel are quoted at AED 180 to 350 by Bestimate and up to AED 500 by independent home tutors; BartyED publishes AED 650 at the premium end.

Every one of those numbers belongs to the provider named beside it and none is an IB Gram price. What they tell an MYP parent is where the money is worth spending. For criterion work, the thing being bought is someone who has read the descriptors enough times to recognise a pattern in six marked tasks. That is a specialist skill and it sits in the middle band, not the top. Paying in-home rates for it buys travel, which changes nothing a student writes. Start with the free trial lesson and a consultation, and judge the diagnosis.

faqs.question: What is the difference between an MYP grade and a percentage?
faqs.answer: An MYP grade is a conversion, not a percentage. Each subject is assessed against four criteria marked out of eight, giving a total out of 32, which is then converted to a grade from 1 to 7 using published bands. A 5 covers a total anywhere from 19 to 23, so two students with the same grade can be four marks apart. That is why the criterion marks matter more than the grade. Ask the school for all four marks each reporting cycle; most provide them as standard and nearly all will on request.

faqs.question: My child holds 5s in MYP but the school says that is not enough for Higher Level. Why?
faqs.answer: Because a 5 spans a wide band and because schools look at which criteria produced it. A student scoring 8, 4, 8, 4 totals 24 and looks solid, but is working at the ceiling on half the subject and has never scored well on investigation or evaluation — the exact behaviours a Higher Level course demands constantly. Ask the school which criterion they are concerned about and what an 7 on it would look like in the next task. That turns a vague judgement into a specific, fixable target.

faqs.question: How are the four MYP criteria actually marked?
faqs.answer: Each criterion has published descriptors in bands, and a teacher judges which band best fits the work, awarding a mark out of eight. The criteria mean different things in different subject groups: criterion C is communicating in mathematics, processing and evaluating in sciences, and producing text in language and literature. The marks are not averaged across tasks mechanically; teachers use their judgement of the student's current best-fit performance. That is why reading the descriptor with your child is more useful than asking for more practice questions.

faqs.question: Does the MYP prepare a child for IGCSE as well as it does for the Diploma?
faqs.answer: It prepares them differently. The Diploma shares the MYP's command terms, its inquiry habits and its internal assessment culture, so the transition is mainly about meeting timed external papers for the first time. IGCSE assumes a body of content in syllabus order and rewards tiered paper technique, which the MYP teaches through inquiry rather than coverage. Neither transition is difficult if the right gap is addressed. The mistake is treating both as the same summer of general revision, which leaves the real difficulty untouched until October.

faqs.question: What is the Personal Project and how much of MYP 5 does it decide?
faqs.answer: It is a self-directed project completed in MYP 5 with a product or outcome, a process journal and a report, assessed against three criteria — planning, applying skills and reflecting — totalling 24 marks. The product itself is not marked. What is marked is the planning, the evidence of skills applied and the quality of reflection. It does not determine the other subject grades, but it is often the first substantial independent piece of work a student produces, and schools use it as evidence about readiness for the Diploma.

faqs.question: May a tutor help with the Personal Project without breaking IB rules?
faqs.answer: Yes, within a firm boundary. A tutor may ask whether a goal is specific enough to evidence, whether success criteria are measurable, whether the journal records decisions rather than activities, and whether a reflection reflects or merely narrates. A tutor may give feedback on a draft the student has written. A tutor may not choose the goal, draft the report, write the reflection or produce any part of the product. Submitting work that is not the student's own is malpractice under IB rules and the consequence falls on the student.

faqs.question: Is criterion D the reason my child's science grade will not move?
faqs.answer: Frequently, yes. Criterion D in sciences asks a student to reflect on the impacts of science, and most students describe an impact rather than evaluating the science behind it. Because each criterion is capped at eight, a strong criterion A cannot compensate indefinitely: once A is at the ceiling, the total cannot rise without D improving. Ask for the four marks across the last three reporting cycles. If D has sat at four or five while A sits at seven or eight, you have found the problem and it is a short piece of work to fix.

faqs.question: Should we move our child from the MYP to IGCSE before Year 10?
faqs.answer: It depends on the destination rather than on which programme is better. If the child is likely to stay in an IB school through the Diploma, staying in the MYP avoids a pointless change of assessment system. If the family may move to a British school or to A Levels, switching before Year 10 avoids arriving mid-course into tiered IGCSE papers. Ask both schools what content they assume at entry, in writing, and decide on that rather than on reputation. Either route works when the gap is planned for.

faqs.question: How much does MYP tutoring cost for a Business Bay family?
faqs.answer: Buy it as a block rather than by the hour, because the usual purchase is six to eight sessions on one criterion. At the published Dubai specialist rates — TutorChase at AED 270 an hour, Bestimate's 2026 table at AED 200 to 450 and above — that block lands roughly between AED 1,200 and AED 3,600. The generalist online band, Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52 and EdFlik from AED 45 to 65, puts a block nearer AED 200 to 520 but rarely buys descriptor expertise. All figures belong to the providers named.

faqs.question: Is an MYP tutor in Downtown Dubai closer to my child's school than an online one?
faqs.answer: Not meaningfully. Downtown has no secondary campus either, so a tutor there is no nearer your child's school than anyone else, and the MYP criteria are identical in every IB school in the city regardless. What a nearby tutor would offer is a car journey you pay for in either time or rate. What an online specialist offers is someone who has read the descriptors for your child's subject group repeatedly. Timing is the only genuinely local variable, and online delivery removes travel at both ends of a weeknight.

faqs.question: Which schools near Business Bay run the MYP rather than IGCSE?
faqs.answer: Business Bay has no campus of its own, so students travel. Several schools in the creek-side cluster run the IB continuum through the MYP, including North London Collegiate School Dubai and Swiss International Scientific School Dubai in the Sobha Hartland and Al Jaddaf direction, while others nearby run a British curriculum to IGCSE and offer the Diploma afterwards. Dubai International Academy Al Barsha is an IB school in the second direction. Those names are context for the school run only; no affiliation or endorsement is implied, and the school's own admissions page is the authority.

faqs.question: What time can an MYP session start on a weeknight in Business Bay?
faqs.answer: Most Business Bay students are home between 15:45 and 16:30 in term time, which makes 17:30 workable and 18:00 comfortable once a snack and some homework have happened. Children commuting from the Jumeirah direction return later and often settle on 18:30. Because lessons are online there is no travel to add at either end, which is the practical advantage of this district. Hold a slightly later slot for the first fortnight, then move it earlier once you know what the bus route actually does in traffic.

faqs.question: Do Business Bay MYP students sit external examinations at the end of MYP 5?
faqs.answer: Only where the school chooses to enter them. The IB offers optional on-screen examinations and ePortfolios in MYP 5 which lead to the IB MYP Certificate, and some schools in Dubai use them while others do not. Ask your school directly, because it changes what MYP 5 preparation should look like: an entered cohort needs timed on-screen practice, while a school using internal assessment alone needs the criterion work to continue. Either way, the Personal Project is completed and the subject criteria are assessed as usual.

faqs.question: How do the Dubai mandatory subjects fit into a Business Bay school's MYP timetable?
faqs.answer: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral studies are required in all Dubai private schools whatever the licensed curriculum, and the emirate's rules require separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students, with combined classes prohibited because the curriculum expectations and language of instruction differ. Instructional time is calculated on a forty-minute lesson unit. The practical effect on an MYP family is that the week contains fewer discretionary hours than the eight subject groups suggest, which is worth counting before adding two tutoring sessions.

faqs.question: What happens if no MYP specialist is free for my child's subject group?
faqs.answer: You are told, with the wait. Coverage for a specific subject group at a specific weeknight hour is not guaranteed, and the honest options are a different slot, a short wait for a named tutor, or a different weekday. What should not happen is being matched to a general tutor described as an MYP specialist, which costs a family several sessions before anyone admits the descriptors are unfamiliar. Asking a provider directly what happens when nobody is available is a reasonable test of any of them, including this one.

intro.heading: Four middle-school systems on one strip of Dubai, and the comparison nobody writes down
paragraphs: City Walk sits in the middle of one of the most curriculum-dense stretches of Dubai. Within a short drive a family can choose between the IB Middle Years Programme, British Key Stage 3 leading to IGCSE, an American middle-school programme, and bilingual or Indian-curriculum provision. Parents move between them, compare notes at the school gate, and arrive at a tutoring enquiry holding a comparison they cannot complete because nobody has set the systems side by side honestly.

That comparison is what this page does, because for a Middle Years Programme family it is the useful work. The MYP does not report percentages. It reports criterion levels and a grade on a different scale from the one most parents grew up with, which means a family can hold a report for three years without knowing whether their child is doing well. Meanwhile the neighbour's child sits IGCSE papers at sixteen with grades everybody recognises, and the comparison feels unfavourable even when the student is thriving.

So we compare four things. The MYP against IGCSE, Key Stage 3 and American middle school, on content, assessment and what each keeps open at sixteen. Criterion levels against the percentage marks a parent understands, with the translation problem named rather than glossed. The eight subject groups against each other, on what a tutor can and cannot usefully do in each. And City Walk against the neighbouring districts, where the honest finding is that the schools differ and the tutoring answer does not.

What a Middle Years Programme tutor actually does follows from that. It is not subject cramming, because there is no external examination to cram for in most MYP years. It is teaching a student to meet published criteria: to write an evaluation where an evaluation is asked for, to reflect rather than summarise, to apply a skill in an unfamiliar context, which is the thing criterion D in most subject groups rewards and the thing most students lose marks on. Confirm the current criteria and descriptors with your child's school, since the IB revises them.

On delivery, plainly. IB Gram teaches UAE families one-to-one over live video. We do not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE and we operate no centre here; home visiting is a service we run only in India. For a middle-school student, sessions are usually shorter than a Diploma student's and are best placed early in the evening rather than late, which the short City Walk school run makes practical. Short frequent sessions are also only economic over video, since nobody drives across Dubai twice a week to teach forty minutes to a twelve year old.

Everything below is sourced where it can be. Regulatory facts are attributed to u.ae and KHDA. Market rates are attributed to the provider or publication that published them, with the month they were read, and none of them is a price of ours. Where a detail of IB assessment could not be verified from an official source it is flagged for confirmation with the school rather than stated as fact, and no statistic appears here without a number, a date and a method behind it.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-city-walk.programmesIntro: A City Walk family is comparing programmes as much as choosing one. These are the four routes in play across this part of Dubai, set out on the same terms so they can actually be compared.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme, MYP 1-5
programmes.description: Five years across eight subject groups, assessed internally against published criteria rather than by annual external examination. Each subject is marked on four criteria, and criterion levels combine into a subject grade on a scale that is not a percentage. The programme emphasises conceptual understanding, inquiry and the transfer of skills to unfamiliar contexts, and culminates in the Personal Project in MYP 5.
programmes.countryNote: Several schools around City Walk, Jumeirah and Umm Suqeim run the MYP through to MYP 5 before the Diploma. Dubai's 2026-27 intake adds three new International Baccalaureate schools among seven new private schools, creating 16,846 new places in total, so the IB share of this corridor is growing rather than static.

programmes.name: British Key Stage 3 into IGCSE
programmes.description: Three years of Key Stage 3 followed by two years of IGCSE, examined externally at sixteen with grades on the 9-1 or A*-G scales. Content coverage is specified and assessment is predominantly by written paper. The comparison most City Walk MYP parents make is with this route, because it dominates the corridor by enrolment and because its grades are legible to everybody.
programmes.countryNote: UK curriculum accounts for 37% of Dubai private school students, against 7% on an International Baccalaureate programme, from a 2024-25 market of 387,441 students across 227 private schools. That asymmetry is why MYP families in this district are usually the ones explaining their child's report rather than reading somebody else's.

programmes.name: American middle school
programmes.description: Three years of middle school with continuous assessment, a grade point average, and a high-school diploma pathway afterwards that may include Advanced Placement courses. Assessment is frequent and percentage-based, which makes progress legible to parents in a way the MYP is not, and which is one reason some families find the transition into the MYP disorienting.
programmes.countryNote: American curriculum accounts for 14% of Dubai private school students. For equivalency purposes the American track has its own sourced requirements: English proficiency via IELTS academic 5, TOEFL iBT 61 or SAT 450 in reading and writing, and SAT Mathematics of at least 450. No IB points threshold has been published on an official source, so none appears here.

programmes.name: The mandatory UAE subjects, in every route
programmes.description: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies run alongside the licensed international curriculum in every Dubai private school, whichever route a family chooses. They occupy timetabled periods and appear on the report, and they are one of the few genuinely common elements across all four systems compared on this page.
programmes.countryNote: KHDA requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited. Instructional time is calculated based on a 40-minute lesson unit, and for these subjects the use of any different or additional content without prior Ministry of Education permission is strictly prohibited.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-city-walk.subjectsIntro: The eight Middle Years Programme subject groups, compared on what a tutor can usefully do in each. The honest answer differs more between groups than families expect, and in two of them the useful work is mostly not tutoring at all.

subjects.name: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Assessed on analysing, organising, producing text and using language. The recoverable work is structural: students who read perceptively still land mid-band because the response is not organised to the criterion. Reading a descriptor together and rewriting one paragraph against it is often worth more than three lessons of content.

subjects.name: Language Acquisition
subjects.description: Assessed on comprehending spoken and written text and on communicating in response. Phases rather than year groups determine the level, which parents frequently misread as a setting decision. Progress here comes from frequency rather than session length, so short regular contact is the pattern that works.

subjects.name: Individuals and Societies
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, investigating, communicating and thinking critically. Criterion D is where marks go: students describe sources rather than evaluating them, and they summarise rather than reaching a judgement. That is a specific teachable move and it transfers directly into IGCSE history or the Diploma later.

subjects.name: Sciences
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating, and reflecting on the impacts of science. The design and evaluation criteria are where most MYP science marks are lost, and they are also the criteria that transfer most usefully into IGCSE practical writing and the Diploma investigation.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts. Extended mathematics in MYP 4 and 5 is the route that keeps IB Mathematics Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level realistic. The fourth criterion, real-life application, is the one that distinguishes a 6 from a 7 and the one least practised.

subjects.name: Design
subjects.description: Inquiring and analysing, developing ideas, creating the solution and evaluating. A process subject where marks come from documenting the process rather than from the final artefact, which is counterintuitive for students and for parents. Tutoring here is almost entirely about documentation discipline.

subjects.name: Arts
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, developing skills, thinking creatively and responding. Like Design, assessed substantially on process and reflection. The useful tutoring intervention is narrow: helping a student articulate a reflection that explains a decision rather than describing what was made.

subjects.name: Physical and Health Education
subjects.description: Assessed on knowing and understanding, planning for performance, applying and performing, and reflecting and improving performance. Tutoring is rarely the right answer here, and saying so is more useful than offering it. Where a student is losing marks it is usually on the written planning and reflection components.

subjects.name: Interdisciplinary units
subjects.description: Assessed across subject groups on disciplinary grounding, synthesising and reflecting. Students find these the hardest thing in the programme because the task does not belong to a subject they can revise. The transferable skill is explicit synthesis, which is teachable and which almost nobody teaches.

subjects.name: The Personal Project
subjects.description: An extended independent project with a written report, assessed against published criteria. The boundary is absolute: a tutor may explain criteria, discuss process and give feedback on the student's own work, and may not write, produce or complete any part of it. Confirm the current criteria with the school's MYP coordinator.

subjects.name: Service as Action
subjects.description: A participation and reflection requirement rather than an assessed subject in the usual sense. Nothing here needs a tutor, and a provider offering support for it is selling something unnecessary. The reflection writing is the only part where a student might need help structuring their thinking.

subjects.name: Approaches to Learning
subjects.description: The skills framework running through the programme: thinking, communication, social, self-management and research skills. This is the genuinely transferable part of the MYP and the thing that makes a well-taught MYP student strong in the Diploma. It is also the part that a subject-focused tutor tends to ignore entirely.

sections.heading: Four middle-school systems, set side by side
paragraphs: This is the comparison a City Walk family is usually making in their head and has never seen written down. Four systems operate within a short drive, they assess completely differently, and they close different doors at sixteen. Putting them on one set of terms is more useful than any amount of advocacy for one of them.

The Middle Years Programme assesses internally against published criteria, reports criterion levels and a subject grade that is not a percentage, and runs five years to MYP 5. British Key Stage 3 into IGCSE assesses mostly by written paper, reports percentages and then external grades at sixteen on a scale everybody recognises. American middle school assesses continuously with a grade point average and leads into a high-school diploma. Bilingual and Indian-curriculum provision adds further variation across the corridor.

What differs most is not rigour but legibility. An MYP report is harder for a parent to read than a percentage, which is why MYP families in this district spend three years uncertain whether their child is doing well while their IGCSE-route neighbours do not. That is an information problem rather than an educational one, and it is solvable in a single conversation with the criteria in front of you.

What differs materially at sixteen is the transition. An MYP 5 student moving into the Diploma is continuing within one philosophy, and the shift from criterion-based coursework to timed unseen papers still catches students out in DP1. An MYP 5 student moving into IGCSE or A Levels is making a larger jump, because external written examination is a skill the MYP does not systematically train. Neither is a reason to avoid the programme; both are reasons to prepare for the specific transition your family is heading towards.

sections.heading: Criterion levels against the marks you already understand
paragraphs: The most common question a City Walk MYP parent asks is what a level 5 actually means, and the honest answer is that it means a band of performance against a published descriptor rather than a proportion of marks earned. Each subject in the Middle Years Programme is assessed against four criteria, each criterion is marked on a scale, and the criterion levels combine into a subject grade on a separate scale. Confirm the exact current structure and boundaries with your child's school, because the IB revises them and schools report in slightly different ways.

The translation problem is real and worth being explicit about. A criterion level is not a percentage and a subject grade is not an IGCSE grade. Treating a 6 as equivalent to a particular percentage or letter will mislead you, and the frequent consequence is a family either relaxing when they should not or buying tutoring they do not need. What a criterion level does tell you, precisely, is which band of a published descriptor the student's work sat in for that criterion on that task.

That precision is also the opportunity. Because the descriptors are published, a student can be taught to read their own work against them, which is something no percentage allows. A student who can look at a piece of their own writing and say that it describes rather than evaluates, and therefore sits in the middle band of that criterion rather than the top, has acquired a skill that will serve them through the Diploma and beyond. That is the central work of Middle Years Programme tutoring.

A practical step that costs nothing. Ask the school for the criterion descriptors for one subject, sit down with your child and the last marked task, and work out together which band each criterion landed in and why. Most families have never done this, and most schools provide the descriptors on request or already publish them in the course guide. It usually takes thirty minutes and it frequently makes a tutor unnecessary in that subject.

sections.heading: City Walk against its neighbours: the schools differ, the answer does not
paragraphs: City Walk has no school inside its boundary, so every family here commutes, and the comparison families make is between campuses rather than between districts. Jumeirah 1 and 2 are the closest and most varied cluster, containing both IB and British provision. Jumeirah 3 and Umm Suqeim hold a further concentration of international schools. Al Wasl and Al Safa are predominantly British curriculum, which is where the IGCSE comparison at the school gate comes from.

Those differences are real and they matter when choosing a school. They do not change the tutoring answer, and it is worth saying why. The Middle Years Programme is assessed against published criteria by the school, which means the useful tutoring work is reading those criteria with the student and applying them to their own tasks. That work is identical whether the campus is in Jumeirah 1 or Umm Suqeim, and it depends entirely on having the school's own unit planner and task sheet rather than on proximity to the building.

Nor does proximity produce a specialist. The MYP has eight subject groups, five year levels and four criteria each, which is a large number of distinct teaching situations spread across a modest number of students in any one district. A parent who filters for a tutor within twenty minutes of City Walk is choosing from a pool of a few dozen; the family's actual requirement, somebody who has taught MYP 4 Individuals and Societies and understands criterion D, is unlikely to be inside it.

The one thing the district genuinely controls is the start time, and here City Walk does well. Short runs in several directions mean an MYP student can often be home by 3.45pm, which supports a 4pm session. For an eleven to fourteen year old that matters more than it does for a Diploma student, because a forty-minute session at 4pm is productive and the same session at 7.30pm frequently is not.

sections.heading: The criterion where most MYP marks actually go
paragraphs: Across the subject groups, the recurring loss is in the criterion that asks a student to do something with knowledge rather than to state it. It appears under different names: evaluating in sciences, thinking critically in Individuals and Societies, applying mathematics in real-life contexts, evaluating in Design. In every case it asks for application, judgement or evaluation in a context the student has not seen before, and in every case students produce description instead.

The pattern is diagnosable from any marked task. A student scoring well on the knowing-and-understanding criterion and poorly on the application criterion does not have a content problem; they have never been taught the shape of an evaluative answer. They write what happened, carefully and correctly, where they were asked what it implies, what the limitation is, or which option is better and why. The content is right and the answer is in the wrong form.

This is also why Middle Years Programme tutoring looks different from subject cramming. There is no annual external paper to drill in most MYP years, so the work is teaching the move: state a judgement, support it with specific evidence, acknowledge the limitation, and connect it back to the question. Taught once properly it transfers across subject groups, which makes it unusually good value: three sessions in one subject frequently improve criterion performance in two others.

For a City Walk family the practical sequence is short. Ask the school for the criterion descriptors in the subject where the levels are lowest. Find the marked task that produced those levels. Identify whether the gap is in knowledge or in the application criterion. If it is application, a short block will move it. If it is knowledge across all four criteria, the conversation belongs with the subject teacher before it belongs with a tutor.

sections.heading: MYP 5 into the Diploma, or into IGCSE: two different jumps
paragraphs: At sixteen a City Walk MYP student goes in one of two directions, and the two require different preparation. Into the Diploma, which is the continuation route and feels like one unbroken course because it often happens on the same campus. Or out to IGCSE or A Levels, usually because of a school move or a family relocation.

The Diploma jump is underestimated precisely because it looks continuous. MYP 5 assessment is criterion-based coursework and tasks; DP1 includes timed unseen papers, and in mathematics and the sciences particularly, a student with strong MYP levels can find October of DP1 genuinely difficult. The demand is new rather than harder. Six to ten weeks of timed practice in the summer or the first term closes most of that gap, and extended mathematics in MYP 4 and 5 is what keeps Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level realistic.

The jump out to IGCSE is larger in a different way. The MYP does not systematically train external written examination, so a student moving into Year 10 or Year 11 of an IGCSE course meets specification content, tiering and past papers all at once. The useful preparation is practical: find out which specification and tier the receiving school will enter them for, obtain the specification, and work through the content gap rather than assuming equivalence between the systems.

In both cases the mistake is to treat the move as administrative. A City Walk family deciding in the spring of MYP 5 which direction to go should ask the receiving school, in writing, what it expects an incoming MYP 5 student to have covered, and where the gaps usually are. Schools answer this well when asked specifically, and the answer turns a vague worry into a six-week piece of work.

sections.heading: The Personal Project compared with IGCSE coursework
paragraphs: Families moving between systems frequently ask how the Personal Project compares with an IGCSE coursework piece, and the comparison is instructive because the two reward almost opposite things. An IGCSE coursework piece is generally judged on the quality of the final output against subject criteria. The Personal Project is judged substantially on the process: the goal, the planning, the documentation and the reflection, with the artefact or outcome as evidence rather than as the whole assessment.

This catches students out in a specific way. A capable MYP 5 student produces an impressive final outcome, documents almost none of the process, and scores in the middle bands. A less impressive outcome with a rigorously documented process and genuine reflection scores higher. That is not a flaw in the assessment; it is what the assessment is for. But it is counterintuitive for a student and for a parent who has been looking at the outcome rather than the process journal.

The boundary on what help is permissible is absolute in both systems and worth stating in the same words. A tutor may explain the criteria, discuss whether a goal is achievable and documentable, and give feedback on the student's own writing and planning. A tutor may not write, produce, draft or complete any part of the work. A malpractice finding falls on the student, and in the IB that can have consequences well beyond one grade. We will not do it and will not accept such work if a family offers it.

The useful intervention is early and small. One or two sessions at the goal-setting stage, establishing whether the proposed project can actually be documented against the criteria, routinely prevents months of work that cannot score well. Confirm the current criteria with your school's MYP coordinator, since the IB revises them, and ask for the school's own guidance document, which will set out its internal deadlines.

sections.heading: What MYP support costs against Diploma support
paragraphs: A useful comparison for a City Walk family is between what middle-school support costs and what Diploma support costs, because the published Dubai rates are generally quoted for the senior end of the market and parents assume they apply throughout.

The published figures, each attributed to the provider or publication that stated it and read in October 2026: Tutopiya advertises from AED 33 to 52 an hour and EdFlik from AED 45 to 65 at the budget end of online tutoring. Unitors publishes IGCSE tuition from AED 150 an hour and IB from AED 200, which is itself a useful comparison because it shows one provider pricing the IB above IGCSE. Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table puts in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to 350 and IB, IGCSE and A-Level specialist work at AED 200 to 450 or more, with independent home tutors reaching AED 200 to 500 once travel is included. TutorChase quotes AED 270 and BartyED AED 650 at the premium end. Monthly packages include AED 799 for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour in-home sessions.

Two observations a City Walk parent can draw from that without help. First, the rates that get quoted in this market are senior-phase rates, and a middle-school session is a different piece of work: shorter, aimed at criterion literacy rather than examination technique, and frequently needing fewer sessions in total. A provider quoting a Higher Level Diploma rate for an MYP 2 student should be asked what the premium is for. Second, Bestimate's monthly estimates for a weekly one-hour session run AED 240 to 600 at the budget end and AED 600 to 1,200 mid-range, which is the realistic band for sustained middle-school support rather than the specialist exam-year band of AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more.

IB Gram does not publish a UAE rate card on these pages and does not present any of these figures as ours. The free trial lesson exists so a family can see the teaching before discussing money, and for an MYP student it is worth taking at the length you intend to book, because a forty-minute session and an hour are genuinely different experiences for a twelve year old. For wider budget context, KHDA confirmed on 22 May 2026 that there would be no increase in private school fees in Dubai for the 2026-27 academic year, under Dubai's second economic incentives package valued at AED 1.5 billion.

sections.heading: Regulation, the mandatory subjects and what we will not claim
paragraphs: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, so they sit alongside the Middle Years Programme exactly as they sit alongside Key Stage 3. KHDA requires separate classes by group: for Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs, and combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited due to the different curriculum expectations and language of instruction. Instructional time is calculated based on a 40-minute lesson unit, with an advised minimum of 25 minutes for any mandatory subject lesson.

One constraint before buying support for these subjects: for the mandatory UAE subjects, the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is strictly prohibited, and KHDA requires schools to ensure that all teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold appropriate KHDA approval to teach those subjects. A provider claiming to deliver an alternative syllabus in these subjects is describing something not permitted.

Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated by permit. The MoHRE private tutor work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and covers teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. MoHRE's service page lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Individuals tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no fine schedule is published, so no amount appears here.

And the claims we decline. IB Gram holds no KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, Ministry of Education, MoHRE, IB or Cambridge accreditation, licence, approval or partnership, and has no office, branch or centre in the United Arab Emirates. In Dubai your child's school is regulated by KHDA, which is responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate; naming a regulator explains what it does and is not a claim of endorsement. We publish no self-asserted rating, no satisfaction percentage and no statistic without a number, a date and a method, and we do not write or complete assessed work of any kind.

sections.heading: Starting from City Walk, with the comparison settled
paragraphs: The cheapest first step is a thirty-minute conversation at your own kitchen table. Ask the school for the criterion descriptors in the subject where your child's levels are lowest, find the marked task that produced those levels, and work out together which band each criterion landed in and why. Most families have never done this and most schools provide the descriptors readily. It frequently makes a tutor unnecessary in that subject, which is a result worth having.

If a tutor is the right answer, bring three things: the school's unit planner or task sheet for the current unit, the criterion descriptors for that subject, and the most recent marked task with its criterion levels. Those three make a diagnosis possible in the first session. Without them, the first two sessions are spent establishing what the school is actually assessing, which is an avoidable cost.

Coverage across the Middle Years Programme subject groups is good in Language and Literature, Individuals and Societies, Sciences and Mathematics, which is where almost all demand sits. Design, Arts, Language Acquisition in less common languages and interdisciplinary support are narrower, and we will say so at the enquiry rather than matching you to somebody approximate. Physical and Health Education is a subject where tutoring is rarely the right answer and we will tell you that too.

On timing: City Walk's short school runs mean a 4pm session is genuinely available here, and for an eleven to fourteen year old that is the difference between a productive forty minutes and a tired one. Forty to forty-five minutes is usually the right length below MYP 4. The free trial lesson should be taken at the hour and the length you intend to book, so the pattern is tested alongside the teaching, and no card is required to take it.

faqs.question: Is the Middle Years Programme better or worse than the IGCSE route our neighbours use?
faqs.answer: They are different rather than ranked, and the useful comparison is what each closes at sixteen. The MYP assesses internally against published criteria across five years and eight subject groups, and leads naturally into the IB Diploma. British Key Stage 3 into IGCSE assesses mostly by external written paper and produces grades everybody recognises. The MYP trains extended independent work better; the IGCSE route trains timed examination better. Neither is a reason to switch, and both are reasons to prepare specifically for whichever transition your family is heading towards.

faqs.question: Why can't I tell from an MYP report whether my child is doing well?
faqs.answer: Because it reports criterion levels and a subject grade rather than percentages, and the scales are not equivalent to anything you grew up with. That is an information problem and it is solvable in one sitting. Ask the school for the criterion descriptors in one subject, take the last marked task, and work out together which band each criterion landed in and why. Most families have never done this and most schools provide the descriptors readily. Confirm the current structure with the school, because the IB revises it.

faqs.question: What does a level 5 in an MYP subject actually represent?
faqs.answer: A band of performance against a published descriptor for that criterion on that task, not a proportion of marks earned. Each subject is assessed against four criteria, each on its own scale, and the levels combine into a subject grade on a separate scale again. Treating a level as a percentage, or a subject grade as an IGCSE grade, will mislead you in both directions: families relax when they should not and buy tutoring when they need not. Ask the school for the exact current boundaries it uses.

faqs.question: My child scores well on knowing and understanding and poorly on the fourth criterion. Why?
faqs.answer: Because that criterion asks them to do something with the knowledge rather than state it, and almost nobody teaches the shape of that answer explicitly. It appears as evaluating in sciences, thinking critically in Individuals and Societies, applying mathematics in real-life contexts, and evaluating in Design. Students write what happened, correctly and carefully, where they were asked what it implies or which option is better and why. The content is right and the form is wrong, which is a three-session fix that transfers across subject groups.

faqs.question: Does living near our school make it easier to find an MYP tutor in this area?
faqs.answer: No, and the arithmetic is the reason. The Middle Years Programme has eight subject groups, five year levels and four criteria each, which is a large number of distinct teaching situations spread across a modest number of students in any one district. A family's real requirement is somebody who has taught, say, MYP 4 Individuals and Societies and understands the critical-thinking criterion. A pool of a few dozen tutors within twenty minutes of City Walk is unlikely to contain that person with a free hour at the time you need.

faqs.question: Would moving from City Walk to Jumeirah or Umm Suqeim change our options?
faqs.answer: It would change the schools available and not the tutoring answer. Those districts hold a different mix of IB and British provision, which matters when choosing a campus. But MYP support is criterion literacy worked from your child's own school unit planners and descriptors, and that work is identical whichever campus produced the documents. The one thing a district genuinely controls is the session start time, and City Walk's short runs in several directions make a 4pm start among the easiest in this part of Dubai.

faqs.question: How long should a tutoring session be for an MYP 2 student?
faqs.answer: Forty to forty-five minutes, placed early in the evening. Eleven to thirteen year olds concentrate well for that length and poorly beyond it, and a shorter productive session beats a longer one that drifts in the final twenty minutes. The hour matters as much as the length: a session at 4pm after a short school run is worth considerably more than the same session at 7.30pm. Take the free trial at the length and hour you intend to use, so both are tested rather than assumed.

faqs.question: Does extended mathematics in MYP 4 matter for the Diploma?
faqs.answer: Yes, materially. Extended mathematics in MYP 4 and 5 is the route that keeps IB Mathematics Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level realistic, because it covers the algebraic depth that course assumes. A student on standard mathematics who later wants Higher Level Analysis and Approaches is carrying a gap into a demanding two-year course. If a quantitative degree is a possibility, raise the extended question in MYP 3 or early MYP 4 rather than discovering it during the Diploma option choices.

faqs.question: Our child has strong MYP levels. Why would DP1 be difficult?
faqs.answer: Because the demand changes rather than the difficulty. MYP 5 assessment is criterion-based coursework and tasks, which rewards investigation, process and communication. DP1 introduces timed unseen papers, which require repeated manipulation of unfamiliar material against a clock, and that is a skill the MYP does not systematically train. A student holding 6s and 7s can therefore be genuinely able and still struggle in October of DP1, particularly in mathematics and the sciences. Six to ten weeks of timed practice closes most of that gap.

faqs.question: What happens if we move our child from the MYP into an IGCSE school at sixteen?
faqs.answer: They meet specification content, tiering and past papers all at once, which is a larger jump than moving into the Diploma. The practical preparation is administrative first: ask the receiving school in writing which specification and tier they will enter your child for, obtain the specification document, and identify the content gap rather than assuming equivalence between the systems. Schools answer this well when asked specifically, and the answer usually turns a vague worry into a defined six-week piece of work.

faqs.question: How does the Personal Project compare with IGCSE coursework?
faqs.answer: They reward nearly opposite things, which catches students out. An IGCSE coursework piece is generally judged on the quality of the final output against subject criteria. The Personal Project is judged substantially on documented process: the goal, the planning, the process journal and the reflection, with the outcome as evidence rather than the whole assessment. A capable student who produces an impressive artefact and documents almost nothing scores in the middle bands. Confirm the current criteria with your school's MYP coordinator.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help my child plan the Personal Project?
faqs.answer: A tutor may explain each criterion, discuss whether a proposed goal is achievable and documentable against them, and give feedback on the student's own writing and planning. A tutor may not write, draft, produce or complete any part of it. That boundary protects your child, because a malpractice finding falls on the student and in the IB can have consequences beyond a single grade. The highest-value intervention is one or two sessions at the goal-setting stage, which routinely prevents months of work that cannot score well.

faqs.question: Does my child take Arabic and Islamic Education alongside the MYP?
faqs.answer: Yes. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, so they sit alongside the MYP exactly as they do alongside Key Stage 3. KHDA requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and combined classes are strictly prohibited. Instructional time is calculated based on a 40-minute lesson unit, with an advised minimum of 25 minutes for any mandatory subject lesson.

faqs.question: Can we get tutoring in Arabic to support the mandatory subjects?
faqs.answer: Within real limits that are worth knowing. For the mandatory UAE subjects, the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is strictly prohibited, and KHDA requires schools to ensure that all teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold appropriate KHDA approval to teach those subjects. A provider claiming to deliver an alternative syllabus in these subjects is describing something not permitted. Support that works from the school's own material is a different matter, and our coverage in these streams is limited rather than comprehensive.

faqs.question: Should MYP tutoring cost the same as Diploma tutoring in Dubai?
faqs.answer: It is worth asking what the premium is for. The published rates quoted in this market are mostly senior-phase rates: Unitors publishes IB tuition from AED 200 an hour and IGCSE from AED 150, and Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table places specialist work at AED 200 to 450 or more. A middle-school session is shorter, aimed at criterion literacy rather than examination technique, and often needs fewer sessions overall. Bestimate's monthly estimates of AED 240 to 600 budget and AED 600 to 1,200 mid are the realistic band for sustained MYP support.

faqs.question: Is there an MYP tutor who could come to our home in City Walk?
faqs.answer: Not from us. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the United Arab Emirates and has no office, branch or tuition centre here; home visiting is a service we run only in India. All UAE tuition is one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. For a middle-school student this has a practical benefit: short frequent sessions of forty minutes are straightforward over video and uneconomic as drives, and short frequent sessions are exactly what a younger student responds to best.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-city-walk.closingHeading: Finish the comparison before you buy anything
dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-city-walk.closingBody: Most City Walk families arrive at a Middle Years Programme enquiry holding an unfinished comparison, and finishing it is free. Ask the school for the criterion descriptors in the subject where levels are lowest. Sit down with your child and the last marked task and work out which band each criterion landed in and why. If the gap is in the application or evaluation criterion, a short block will move it and we can tell you what that looks like. If the levels are low across all four criteria, the conversation belongs with the subject teacher first. And if the comparison you are really making is between the MYP and the IGCSE route at a neighbouring school, that is a school conversation rather than a tutoring one, and we will say so. The trial lesson is free and no card is required.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-culture-village.tutorsIntro: These are the tutors covering the Middle Years Programme for families in Culture Village: matched to the subject group and the criterion, working to the school's reporting dates, and able to say which marks are still live.

intro.heading: No exam calendar, so work to the reporting cycle
paragraphs: The Middle Years Programme has no external examination in most of its years, which changes everything about how support should be timed. There is no single date to count back from. Instead there is a reporting cycle: tasks set and assessed across each term, criteria judged repeatedly, marks recorded, and a year-end judgement made from the whole pattern rather than from an average. A tutoring plan that treats the MYP like a linear examined course will consistently arrive at the wrong moment.

The structure is the key to the timing. Every subject carries four criteria, labelled A to D, each marked out of eight, giving thirty-two marks that the school converts into a grade from one to seven using published boundaries. Each criterion is then assessed more than once across a year. A student who scored three on criterion C in November may be assessed on criterion C again in February and in April, and the later evidence usually matters more because the judgement is about where the student is by the end.

That has a direct consequence for buying support. The useful question is not what the report said but which criteria are being assessed next, and in which subjects. A parent who asks the school for the assessment schedule, not just the report, can place a short block of work immediately before a criterion is reassessed. That is the highest-return timing available in the programme and almost nobody uses it, because reports arrive after the fact and feel like the end of something.

The other calendar feature that matters is the Personal Project in MYP 5. It runs across most of the final year with school-set stages, and it fails in predictable ways that are visible months ahead. Scope is the dominant failure: a project too ambitious to finish and document arrives at the deadline with an incomplete product and thin process evidence, and the criteria reward documented process heavily. Two hours at the start prevent an outcome twelve hours at the end cannot repair.

In Dubai there are additional calendar items that belong in the week before anything is added. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum. KHDA calculates mandatory-subject instructional time on a forty-minute lesson unit, advises that any such lesson should be at least twenty-five minutes, and requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab pupils in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies.

IB Gram does not send tutors to homes in Culture Village or anywhere else in the UAE. Tuition for UAE families is one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, and home visiting is a service we operate only in India. For the Middle Years Programme the practical benefit is scheduling: a short block timed to land in the fortnight before a criterion is reassessed requires availability at short notice, and that is easier from a national pool than from a visiting diary built on geography.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-culture-village.programmesIntro: Culture Village families reach us at four points in the Middle Years Programme, and the calendar behaves differently at each. These are the stages we cover.

programmes.name: The early years
programmes.description: Eight subject groups taught with an inquiry framework and assessed against four criteria each. No external examination, frequent task-based assessment, and the years in which criteria literacy is either built or missed. A student who learns to read a task sheet and identify which criterion it assesses has an advantage that compounds for five years.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai these years also carry the mandatory UAE subjects alongside the licensed curriculum, and KHDA requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab pupils in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies. For a Culture Village family the practical point is weekly capacity: a Year 8 timetable with those periods plus eight subject groups leaves limited evening room, and overloading it produces diminishing returns quickly.

programmes.name: The year the criteria sharpen
programmes.description: Subject criteria become more demanding in the upper achievement bands, and the gap between a five and a six usually concerns independence and critical thinking rather than coverage. This is the year in which a criterion-level weakness, if it has not been named, starts to look like a general ability judgement instead.
programmes.countryNote: MYP 4 is the cheapest year in which to act and the one families most often skip, because the Personal Project has not arrived and nothing feels urgent. A criterion weakness named here costs a short block. The same weakness in MYP 5, competing with the Personal Project and with a Diploma or IGCSE transition conversation, costs considerably more for the same result.

programmes.name: The final year and the Personal Project
programmes.description: The last year of the programme, carrying the Personal Project with its product, process journal and report, plus subject criteria at their most demanding. Some schools offer optional on-screen eAssessment and ePortfolios leading to the MYP Certificate, which adds external dates to a year that otherwise has none.
programmes.countryNote: Where a school offers eAssessment, it introduces the only genuinely external deadline most MYP students meet, and it should be confirmed with the school early because it changes the shape of the year substantially. Where a school does not, MYP 5 remains an internally assessed year and the Personal Project stages are the fixed points a tutoring plan should be built around.

programmes.name: What comes after MYP
programmes.description: Culture Village students leave the Middle Years Programme for the IB Diploma or, at some schools, into IGCSE and then a post-16 route. Both destinations are examined by timed written papers, which most MYP students have never sat, and both carry internally assessed components with their own criteria.
programmes.countryNote: The transition is the single strongest argument for MYP support, and it has nothing to do with the MYP grade. Investigating patterns in mathematics maps onto the Diploma's Exploration, worth twenty per cent of the maths grade. Inquiring and designing, and processing and evaluating, in sciences map onto the Diploma's scientific investigation, also twenty per cent. Strengthening those criteria in MYP 4 is the cheapest preparation available for either.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-culture-village.subjectsIntro: The eight MYP subject groups, each with the criterion that most often costs marks and the point in the year it is usually assessed.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts. Investigating patterns is the usual loss, because generalising a rule and justifying it is a different skill from computing correctly and is rarely taught explicitly.

subjects.name: Sciences
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating, and reflecting on the impacts of science. Processing and evaluating is where marks go: data collected competently and then discussed without reference to anomalies, validity or improvement.

subjects.name: Language and literature
subjects.description: Analysing, organising, producing text, and using language. Organising is the standing loss, because a sound argument delivered in a structure the reader cannot follow caps the achievement band regardless of the quality of thought behind it.

subjects.name: Individuals and societies
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, investigating, communicating, and thinking critically. Thinking critically is what separates a six from a seven: using sources to build an argument rather than to illustrate a narrative, and recognising a source's limitations.

subjects.name: Language acquisition
subjects.description: Listening, reading, speaking and writing, with phase placement mattering more than year group. A student moved up a phase mid-year frequently loses marks in speaking first, before the other three skills catch up with the new demand.

subjects.name: Design
subjects.description: Inquiring and analysing, developing ideas, creating the solution, and evaluating. Documentation carries the marks here: a strong product with thin process evidence scores below a modest product that is fully documented, which surprises most students.

subjects.name: Arts
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, developing skills, thinking creatively, and responding. The process journal is an assessed artefact as much as the finished work, and students who keep it weekly outperform those who assemble it in the final fortnight.

subjects.name: Physical and health education
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, planning for performance, applying and performing, and reflecting and improving performance. The written and reflective criteria are where marks are available to students who are not the strongest performers.

subjects.name: The Personal Project
subjects.description: An independent project with a product, a process journal and a report, assessed against criteria covering planning, applying skills and reflecting. Scope control decides the outcome: a project narrow enough to finish and document beats an ambitious one abandoned.

subjects.name: Interdisciplinary units
subjects.description: Units drawing on two or more subject groups, assessed against their own criteria. Frequently the lowest marks on a report because students treat them as an add-on rather than as an assessed task with its own requirements.

sections.heading: The MYP year as a reporting cycle
paragraphs: Because there is no external examination in most MYP years, the year has a different shape from an IGCSE or Diploma year. Tasks are set and assessed across each term, criteria are judged repeatedly, and a year-end grade is produced from the pattern of evidence rather than from a single paper. There is no date to count backwards from, which is why families who are used to examined courses find MYP support hard to time.

The shape that replaces it is a cycle with three useful positions. Before a criterion is assessed, when a short block of targeted work can change the mark that gets recorded. Immediately after a report, when the evidence of what went wrong is freshest and the next assessment is still some weeks away. And at the end of a year, when nothing can be changed and the only useful conversation is about the year ahead.

Most families buy support in the third position, because that is when the report arrives and prompts action. It is the least effective of the three. The second position is better, and the first is best, because it places the work immediately before the mark that will be recorded. Getting there requires one thing the school holds and most parents never request: the assessment schedule showing which criteria are assessed when, in which subjects.

The table below sets out the cycle. Dates are deliberately absent because every school sets its own, and a page guessing at them would be useless. What is stable is the shape, and the shape is what tells a Culture Village parent which position in the cycle they are currently standing in.

sections.heading: Criteria are assessed more than once, so marks stay live
paragraphs: This is the single most useful fact about MYP support and it is rarely explained to parents. Each criterion in each subject is assessed more than once across a year, through different tasks. A student who scored three on criterion C in a November task may be assessed on criterion C again in February and again in April. The year-end judgement is formed from that pattern, with later evidence typically carrying more weight because the question is where the student is by the end.

What follows is a timing strategy rather than a volume strategy. If criterion C is the weakness and criterion C is assessed again in six weeks, a short block of work placed in the fortnight before that task does something concrete: it changes a mark that will count. The same block of work placed immediately after a report, with the next criterion C task three months away, is still useful but far less of it survives to the recorded evidence.

The information needed is specific and free. Ask the school which criteria the next assessed task in each subject covers. Many MYP schools publish this in task sheets or in a term overview and will share it readily. With it, a Culture Village family can place a three-session block precisely, which is cheaper than a term of weekly support and more likely to show up in the next report.

One honest qualification. Not every criterion recurs in every subject in every year, and schools vary in how they weight earlier against later evidence. The question to ask is therefore specific: will this criterion be assessed again this year, and how is the year-end judgement formed. A school that cannot answer either question is unusual, and either answer tells a family where they stand.

sections.heading: The Personal Project across MYP 5, stage by stage
paragraphs: The Personal Project is the one part of the Middle Years Programme with a genuine timeline, and it is the component where good timing is worth most. It runs across most of MYP 5 with school-set stages: a topic and goal agreed, a plan written, the product developed, a process journal maintained throughout, and a report submitted. The supervisor is a member of school staff and the work must be the student's own.

Almost every Personal Project that goes wrong goes wrong at the first stage. A goal too ambitious to finish and document in the time available produces a final weeks with an incomplete product and thin process evidence. The criteria reward documented process substantially, so an unfinished ambitious project scores below a completed modest one. Two hours of scope conversation when the project is introduced prevents an outcome that twelve hours at the end cannot repair.

The process journal is the second predictable failure and it is purely a habit. It is an assessed artefact, not a formality, and it is supposed to record decisions and reflections as they happen. A student who writes in it weekly produces evidence the criteria can reward. A student who assembles it in the final fortnight produces a retrospective narrative that reads as exactly that, and the reflection marks go accordingly.

The honesty boundary needs stating before any of this begins, because deadline pressure is when it gets tested. A tutor may discuss scope, ask questions about a plan, explain what a criterion is asking for in plain language, and give feedback on the student's own draft and journal. A tutor may not write the report, restructure it to a standard, or supply the product. Providers in this market sell completed internal assessments, and the consequence of that falls on the student.
