sections.heading: Criterion marking, and why a level 5 on its own tells you nothing
paragraphs: Each subject group has four criteria, lettered A to D, each marked out of eight. The four marks total 32 and the school converts that total to a level from one to seven against published boundaries. What the letters stand for differs by subject group, and this is where most of the confusion in a DIFC household originates: criterion B in mathematics is investigating patterns, criterion B in sciences is inquiring and designing, and criterion B in language and literature is organizing. A parent comparing two subjects' criterion B marks is comparing nothing.

The practical consequence is that a report has to be read column by column. The table below sets out the four criteria for the subject groups DIFC families ask about most, with the thing parents most commonly misread about each. Two patterns recur across every school in this catchment. First, able students score highly on the knowing-and-understanding criterion and lose the level elsewhere, which looks like underachievement and is actually a skills gap. Second, the criteria that are hardest to improve alone, investigating, designing, evaluating and communicating, are precisely the ones a group revision class cannot touch.

There is a question worth asking at the next parents' evening, and it is more useful than asking how the child is getting on. Ask which criterion the subject teacher would prioritise for the next unit and what a mark of six on it would look like compared with the four the child currently has. Teachers can answer that precisely, because the descriptors are published and they use them weekly. The answer converts a vague worry into a specific target, and a specific target is something a forty-minute session can be built on.

rows: Strong arithmetic hides a weak B and D
C predicts Diploma data questions, not A
Good readers often lose the level on B
The phase placement matters more than the marks

sections.heading: The afternoon a DIFC middle-schooler actually has
paragraphs: Session length and start time matter more at this age than at any other, and almost no tutoring provider adjusts for it. A Diploma student can work at eight in the evening because they have to. An eleven-year-old cannot, and a parent who books that slot is paying for attendance rather than learning. The variable that decides everything is when the child walks through the door, which in DIFC means the campus, the finish time and the return leg across Al Khail or Sheikh Zayed Road at the worst part of the afternoon.

The table below is a planning tool rather than an official statement; finish times are set by each school and change by term and by year group, so confirm your own. What it is for is the last two columns. For MYP 1 to MYP 3, forty minutes starting at 16:30 or 17:00 is the shape that works, and the session should finish while there is still evening left for school homework rather than competing with it. For MYP 4 and MYP 5, a full fifty-five minutes at 17:00 or 17:30 is realistic, and a second short session before a criterion-marked assessment is sustainable for a few weeks at a time.

Two practical notes from this cluster. Saturday and Sunday mornings are substantially better than weekday evenings for this age group, and families whose school run comes from Al Sufouh or Nad Al Sheba should go straight to a weekend slot rather than attempting a weekday one and failing at it for a month. And a session that moves by a day costs nothing when it is delivered over video, which means a swimming gala or a school trip reschedules the lesson rather than cancelling it.

table.caption: REALISTIC SESSION WINDOW BY YEAR GROUP, DIFC
rows: 55 minutes, plus a short second session in assessment weeks

sections.heading: The Personal Project, and where MYP 5 students lose it
paragraphs: The Personal Project runs through MYP 5 and is marked out of 24 against three criteria: planning, applying skills, and reflecting, each out of eight. Students consistently misjudge where the marks are. The product, the thing they will show their family, carries far less weight than the process journal and the report that describe how it was made and what was learned. A beautifully built product with a thin journal lands on a middling mark every single time, and the student is genuinely surprised.

The failure mode is almost always criterion A. A goal is chosen because it sounds interesting rather than because it can be assessed: too broad, with no stated criteria for success, and no realistic plan for the time available. By December the work has started, the journal has four entries written on one afternoon, and nothing can be reconstructed. The fix is cheap and has to be early. One or two sessions interrogating the goal, defining what success would look like, and establishing a journal habit of five minutes after every working session is worth more than ten hours in February.

The boundary on help is the same as everywhere else on this site and we state it plainly rather than leaving it implied. A tutor may teach what each criterion rewards, ask whether a goal is specific enough to assess, press on whether a journal entry shows real reflection rather than description, and explain what the report has to demonstrate. A tutor may not write, edit, restructure or supply the journal, the report or the product, and may not choose the goal. The student's name on that work has to mean something, and Dubai schools run originality checks and supervisor declarations on it.
bullets: Three criteria, planning, applying skills and reflecting, eight marks each
The process journal and report outweigh the product
Criterion A failures cannot be repaired after the work has started
Five minutes of journalling after each working session is the whole habit

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies alongside the programme
paragraphs: This is the part of a Dubai middle-school timetable that no tutoring page in this market explains, and it has a direct effect on where a student's week goes. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the international curriculum the school is licensed to teach, and KHDA's requirements were to be implemented by the start of the 2025-26 academic year, or April 2026 for schools whose year begins in April. They are not optional extras and they are not inside the eight Middle Years Programme subject groups.

The organisational rules are specific, and parents are often unaware of them. KHDA requires separate classes by group: for Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs, and combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because the curriculum expectations and language of instruction differ. Standard Arabic is required as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arab students and for Arabic as a first language; Arabic is the primary language for Social Studies for Arab students; and the school's licensed-curriculum language is used for non-Arabs in Islamic Education and in moral, social and cultural studies.

Two further details are worth knowing. Schools are required to ensure that all teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold appropriate KHDA approval to teach those subjects, which is a credential a parent can reasonably ask about. And instructional time for the mandatory subjects is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit, with schools permitted to vary lesson length provided the total weekly time is met and with a recommendation that any mandatory-subject lesson runs at least 25 minutes. For the mandatory subjects, using different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is strictly prohibited, which is a real constraint on how any Arabic or Islamic Education support can be described, and we describe ours as practice and language work aligned to what the school is already teaching.
bullets: Mandatory in all Dubai private schools whatever curriculum is licensed
Separate classes for Arab and non-Arab pupils; combined classes prohibited
Teachers of Arabic and Islamic Education need appropriate KHDA approval
Instructional time is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit

sections.heading: MYP 5 into the Diploma, and the gaps that surface in Year 12
paragraphs: Students coming out of MYP 5 arrive in the Diploma with real advantages and two predictable deficits, and knowing which is which saves a family a wasted term. The advantages are genuine: inquiry structure, comfort with extended independent work, fluency in command terms, and a process-documentation habit that makes internal assessments considerably less frightening than they are for students arriving from a purely examined route. The science investigation and the Extended Essay both reward exactly what the Middle Years Programme spent five years building.

The deficits are examination stamina and drilled content recall. A student who has been assessed through criterion-marked tasks has rarely sat a two-hour written paper under timed conditions with no resources, and the first Year 12 mock is often a shock that has nothing to do with understanding. Alongside that, criterion-based assessment does not reward volume of recall in the way a Year 11 qualification does, so a Middle Years Programme student may know how to think about a topic without being able to retrieve the facts quickly. Both are habit problems and both respond to a few weeks of deliberate work.

The cheapest time to do that work is the summer between MYP 5 and Year 12, and the specific content to prioritise depends on the subjects chosen. For the sciences it is quantitative fluency: moles, concentration, unit handling, uncertainties and reading a gradient. For mathematics it is algebraic speed, because both Diploma mathematics courses assume rearrangement happens quickly and without thought. For the essay subjects it is timed writing, which nothing in the Middle Years Programme required. Six weeks spent there is the least expensive and most effective Diploma preparation available, and it is bought before anything has gone wrong.
bullets: Advantages carried forward: inquiry, independence, command terms, documentation
Deficits to expect: timed examination stamina and fast content recall
Priority summer work: quantitative fluency, algebraic speed, timed writing
Extended mathematics in MYP 4 and 5 is the route into Higher Level Analysis and Approaches

sections.heading: Online delivery, the permit, and the claims we will not make
paragraphs: Middle Years Programme lessons for UAE families are delivered one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time. Nobody is sent to a DIFC address. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; in-home tutoring is a service that exists only in India. For a younger student the online format has a specific advantage that is worth naming: because no journey has to be paid for, a session can be forty minutes instead of sixty, which matches the attention span of an eleven-year-old far better than an hour does. Market rates for in-home work in Dubai run roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour against AED 150 to 300 for qualified online tutors, and the difference is a car rather than better teaching.

Private tuition in the UAE is permitted and regulated, and the honest position is worth stating because most of this market stays quiet about it. An individual giving private lessons needs a private tuition work permit from the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation, introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. It is granted free of charge for two years, applied for through MoHRE's 'Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing' service via the ministry's app, website and e-services system, and open to teachers registered at government or private schools, government and private sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Anyone tutoring without one is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and because no schedule of amounts has been published, none is quoted here.

The things we decline to claim are as follows. IB Gram is not approved, accredited, certified or licensed by KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, the Ministry of Education, the IB organisation, Cambridge or Pearson, and nothing on this page should be read as implying otherwise; a KHDA educational services permit is issued to training institutes with premises and we do not hold one. We have no office, centre or branch in the UAE. No tutor can guarantee a level, a grade or a Personal Project mark, because those are awarded by the school against published criteria and moderated by the programme. And no statistic appears on this page without its source and date, which is a lower bar than it should be in this market and one most of the pages competing for this search do not clear.
bullets: Online, one-to-one, Gulf Standard Time; no UAE home visits, India only
Forty-minute sessions are possible precisely because nobody travels
MoHRE private tuition permit: free of charge, two years, Resolution No. 710 of 2023
No regulator accreditation claimed, no UAE premises, no guaranteed levels

process.title: Send the report, not a summary of it
process.description: The criterion breakdown is the diagnostic, so send the actual report with the four marks per subject rather than the overall levels. Add the school, the Middle Years Programme year, and the two afternoon windows that are genuinely free after the drive back into DIFC. That is enough to shortlist a tutor who can read the marks properly.

process.title: A diagnostic session at no charge
process.description: Forty to fifty-five minutes depending on age, no card details taken. The tutor works through a recent criterion-marked task and asks the student to explain their own thinking, then writes a short note naming which criterion is actually costing the level and whether the gap is knowledge, structure or habit.

process.title: One criterion as the target, with the teacher's own wording
process.description: The plan names a single criterion and what a higher mark on it would look like in this subject at this school. Where possible we use the subject teacher's own description of the next unit's priority, because the descriptors are published and the teacher applies them weekly. A vague worry becomes a target a forty-minute session can hit.

process.title: Short sessions, early, with a note each time
process.description: Forty minutes at 16:30 for the younger years, fifty-five later. Every session ends with two named priorities and one task small enough to actually be done. Parents get that note rather than a score, so the next parents' evening is a conversation about specifics rather than about effort.

process.title: Reassess at the reporting cycle, and stop when it is done
process.description: The school's next report is the honest checkpoint. If the targeted criterion has moved, the plan either moves to the next one or ends. A tutor who recommends continuing indefinitely is not reading the marks, and a Middle Years Programme intervention that finishes after a term because it worked is the intended outcome rather than a lost customer.

whyPoints.title: Tutors who can read a criterion report
whyPoints.description: Criterion B means investigating patterns in mathematics, inquiring and designing in sciences and organizing in language and literature. A tutor who does not know that cannot tell you which strand is costing the level, and most of the value in Middle Years Programme support is in that diagnosis rather than in the teaching that follows.

whyPoints.title: Sessions sized for the age, not for the invoice
whyPoints.description: Forty minutes for MYP 1 to MYP 3, starting at 16:30 while the child is still alert. That is possible because nobody is driving anywhere, and it is the main practical reason online delivery suits this age group better than an in-home visit that has to be an hour to be worth the journey.

whyPoints.title: The Personal Project kept the student's own
whyPoints.description: Criteria taught, goals interrogated, journal habits built, reflection pressed on. Nothing written, edited or supplied, and we say that here rather than in the terms. The providers in this market that blur the line are putting a student's MYP certificate and later diploma at risk, not their own position.

whyPoints.title: The Dubai mandatory subjects taken seriously
whyPoints.description: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies are required in every Dubai private school and occupy real timetable and homework time, with separate classes for Arab and non-Arab pupils and prescribed languages of instruction. A support plan that ignores them is planning a week that does not exist.

whyPoints.title: The transition planned rather than survived
whyPoints.description: Entering the Middle Years Programme from another system and leaving MYP 5 for the Diploma are both predictable, and both have known deficits attached. We name them, say which weeks to use, and say what the specific content priorities are rather than selling a general course of sessions across the gap.

whyPoints.title: Availability limits stated before you pay
whyPoints.description: Early-evening slots in this district are genuinely finite, and in some subject groups and language phases the specialist pool is small. If we cannot cover what you need at the hour you need, we will say so and name the alternative rather than putting a generalist in front of a criterion-marked task.

faqs.question: What does MYP 3 mean, and which Dubai school year is my child actually in?
faqs.answer: The Middle Years Programme runs five years, MYP 1 to MYP 5, covering roughly ages eleven to sixteen. In most Dubai schools MYP 1 sits alongside Year 7, MYP 2 with Year 8, MYP 3 with Year 9, MYP 4 with Year 10 and MYP 5 with Year 11, although labels vary slightly between campuses and some schools begin the programme at a different point. Confirm with your own school rather than assuming. The practical significance is that MYP 3 is the last year before subject choices narrow, which makes it the sensible point to decide honestly about extended mathematics.

faqs.question: Why does my child's Middle Years Programme report give a 6 in science but no percentage?
faqs.answer: Because the programme does not use percentages. Each subject group is marked against four criteria, each out of eight, and the total out of 32 is converted to a level from one to seven using boundaries the school publishes. The level is a summary, and on its own it conceals the information you need. A child on 7, 4, 4, 5 and a child on 4, 6, 6, 4 can both land on the same level while needing completely different help. Ask the school for the four criterion marks per subject, which is what any useful conversation about support has to start from.

faqs.question: What are the four criteria in Middle Years Programme mathematics marked out of?
faqs.answer: Eight marks each, for a total of 32. The four are knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts. Most students in this catchment score well on knowing and understanding, because that is what their homework and their parents' expectations focus on, and lose the level on investigating patterns and real-life application. Those two reward a type of work that is rarely practised at home: finding and justifying a general rule, and modelling a messy situation. Communicating covers notation, working and explanation, and is often the quickest single mark to recover.

faqs.question: How long should a tutoring session be for an MYP 2 student in DIFC?
faqs.answer: Forty minutes, starting at 16:30 or 17:00. A twelve-year-old who finishes school at about 15:00 and is home in the towers by half past three has roughly one good block of concentration left, and it is not at 18:30. Forty focused minutes while they are alert produce more than an hour when they are not, and finishing early leaves the evening for school homework rather than putting the two in competition. This is practical precisely because the lesson is delivered over video: no journey has to be paid for, so the session can be sized to the child.

faqs.question: Is the Personal Project graded, and does it affect the Diploma?
faqs.answer: It is assessed out of 24 against three criteria, planning, applying skills and reflecting, each worth eight marks, and the school reports a level for it. It does not feed into Diploma points, so it does not affect a university application directly. What it does affect is the student, because it is the first substantial independent piece they will produce and the habits it builds or fails to build reappear in the science investigation and the Extended Essay two years later. Students consistently over-invest in the product and under-invest in the process journal, which is where most of the mark sits.

faqs.question: Does the Middle Years Programme prepare a child for IGCSE if we change schools in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Yes, with one adjustment. The content gap between MYP 3 and the start of a Year 10 IGCSE course is narrower than parents fear, and in the sciences and mathematics it is largely a matter of sequence rather than of missing material. The real gap is examination behaviour: a Middle Years Programme student has usually been assessed through criterion-marked tasks rather than through long timed written papers with no resources. Build that first. A few weeks of timed past-paper practice over a Dubai school holiday removes most of the problem before the new school year starts.

faqs.question: My child is moving from British Year 8 into MYP 3. What actually changes?
faqs.answer: Three things, and none of them is content. Marking changes from percentages and ranks to four criterion marks out of eight per subject. Assessment changes from tests to criterion-marked tasks, several of which are extended pieces with process documentation attached. And the language changes: command terms and inquiry structure are used precisely and the descriptors are published, so a student who answers a question loosely loses marks regardless of how much they know. The first report after a move is usually worse than the child's real ability, and that is a translation problem rather than a decline.

faqs.question: Which Middle Years Programme subject group causes DIFC families the most trouble?
faqs.answer: Sciences, and specifically criterion C, processing and evaluating. It assesses data handling, graphing and the evaluation of results rather than recall, so a student who knows the content well can sit on a 4 and nobody can see why. It also matters more than the other strands for what comes next, because the Diploma sciences examine exactly that skill in their data-based questions and their internally assessed investigation. Individuals and societies criterion D, thinking critically, runs it close, and is the hardest of all the strands to improve without someone questioning the student's reasoning out loud.

faqs.question: Does my child have to take Arabic alongside the Middle Years Programme in a Dubai school?
faqs.answer: Yes. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, and KHDA required its arrangements to be implemented from the start of the 2025-26 academic year, or April 2026 for schools whose year begins in April. Schools must organise separate classes for Arab and non-Arab pupils, and combined classes are strictly prohibited because curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ. Teachers of Arabic and Islamic Education are required to hold appropriate KHDA approval. These lessons occupy timetable and homework time that any support plan has to account for.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with an interdisciplinary unit?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is often where the most useful work happens, because interdisciplinary units ask students to connect two subject groups and most have never been taught how. The teachable part is the structure: identifying what each discipline contributes, where the concepts genuinely overlap rather than merely coexist, and how to show that connection explicitly rather than writing two separate halves. The work itself, the research and the product, remains the student's. One session on the structure before the unit begins tends to be worth more than several after the draft exists.

faqs.question: Is a session straight after school a good idea for a twelve-year-old?
faqs.answer: Not immediately after the door closes, no. A child who walks in at 15:40 needs food, a change of clothes and twenty minutes of nothing before anything useful goes in, so 16:30 is the realistic earliest for an MYP 1 or MYP 2 student in DIFC. Later than about 18:00 the returns fall away quickly at this age. Families with a long return leg from Al Sufouh or Nad Al Sheba should skip the weekday attempt entirely and take a Saturday or Sunday morning slot, where attention is markedly better and a longer session becomes possible.

faqs.question: Does Middle Years Programme eAssessment matter for a student in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Only if your school enters candidates for it, and many do not. The optional on-screen examinations and ePortfolios at the end of MYP 5 lead to an IB MYP certificate, which is a recognition of the five years rather than an entry qualification that universities ask for. Ask the school directly whether it registers students, because the answer changes how MYP 5 should be planned: a cohort sitting eAssessments needs examination practice in a way that a cohort finishing on internal criterion marking does not. Do not assume either way from what the programme looks like elsewhere.

faqs.question: How do we tell whether a level 4 is a problem or completely normal?
faqs.answer: Look at the four criterion marks rather than the level, and then ask the subject teacher one question: which criterion would they prioritise in the next unit, and what would a six on it look like compared with the child's current mark. Teachers can answer that precisely because the descriptors are published and they apply them weekly. A level 4 built on 6, 3, 3, 5 is a specific, fixable skills gap. A level 4 built on 4, 4, 4, 4 is a different conversation about pace and engagement. The level alone cannot distinguish between them.

faqs.question: What should an MYP 5 student do in the summer before the Diploma?
faqs.answer: Two things, and neither is reading ahead. Build examination stamina, because criterion-marked tasks have not required sitting a long written paper under timed conditions with no resources, and the first Year 12 mock is otherwise a shock. Then build quantitative fluency in whatever subjects are coming: moles, concentration, units, uncertainties and reading a gradient for the sciences, and fast algebraic rearrangement for either mathematics course. For essay subjects, timed writing. Six weeks spent there is the cheapest and most effective Diploma preparation available, and it is bought before anything has gone wrong.

faqs.question: How does a Middle Years Programme lesson actually work over video for a younger child?
faqs.answer: The tutor and the student share a screen with the task on it, the student works while the tutor watches the working rather than the finished answer, and the tutor annotates in real time. For criterion-marked tasks the descriptors sit alongside the work so the student can see which strand they are currently satisfying. Sessions are forty minutes at this age, which keeps attention intact. Parents are welcome in the room for the first session and most choose not to be by the third. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes in the UAE; that service exists only in India.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-difc.closingHeading: Start with the criterion marks, not the level
dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-difc.closingBody: Send the actual report with its four criterion marks per subject, tell us the school and the Middle Years Programme year, and name the two afternoon windows that are genuinely free after the drive back into DIFC. The first session carries no charge and takes no card details, and it will be forty minutes if your child is in MYP 1 to MYP 3. Afterwards you get a short written note saying which criterion is costing the level and whether the gap is knowledge, structure or habit. If the honest answer is that the report is normal for the stage and nothing needs buying, the note will say that instead.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-discovery-gardens.tutorsIntro: These are the tutors a Discovery Gardens family is matched with for Middle Years work. The first question any of them should ask is when the next assessed task falls, not what the last report said.

intro.heading: A programme with no exams and a real calendar
paragraphs: The Middle Years Programme has no external examinations until the optional assessments at the very end, and parents reasonably conclude that it therefore has no deadlines worth planning around. It has plenty. Criteria are assessed task by task through the year, each task producing a mark out of eight against published descriptors. Reports summarise those marks, which means a report tells you about tasks that are already finished and graded.

That single fact explains why Middle Years tutoring is so often bought at the least useful moment. A report arrives, the numbers are middling, a family makes contact, and the work begins two weeks later on content rather than on the next assessed task. Meanwhile the next criterion-marked piece is set and submitted without anybody having looked at what the criterion actually asks for.

Timed differently, the same money does far more. A session in the week a task is set, spent reading the criterion descriptors against the task sheet, changes the mark on that task. A session two weeks after a report, spent revising the unit, changes nothing measurable. The difference is not the tutor or the subject but where in the cycle the hour lands, and that is knowable in advance from the school.

Discovery Gardens shapes the practical side helpfully. It is a high-density apartment community of 291 buildings in themed districts beside Ibn Battuta, with its own Route 2020 metro station. Middle Years students here are home earlier than their Diploma siblings, often by 16:00 on the nearest routes, so a 16:30 session is genuinely available rather than theoretical.

IB Gram delivers one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time between 15:30 and 21:30, and no tutor attends a UAE address; home visiting is a service we offer only in India. For Middle Years work the practical requirement is modest: a desk, headphones and the marked task to hand, which suits a community where a spare study is rare. Over-ear headphones solve the noise and a household agreement that the hour is a timetabled lesson solves the interruptions, which is the part no equipment addresses.

One framing point before the detail. Almost everything that follows argues for fewer tutoring hours rather than more, placed where the assessment cycle still allows them to reach a mark. A diagnosis session on marked work, then two or three attached to specific upcoming tasks, resolves most single-criterion problems at this stage. The arrangements that run all year without visible change are usually standing weekly hours bought in response to a report and spent revising content that was never the problem.

The rest of this page sets out the Middle Years year as a calendar: when criteria are actually assessed, how the Personal Project timeline runs across MYP 4 and 5, where the optional MYP 5 assessments sit and whether your school uses them, how Ramadan and the UAE breaks affect this stage, and what the final two years should be building towards.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-discovery-gardens.programmesIntro: The Middle Years Programme spans five years and its calendar changes character as it goes. These are the phases a Discovery Gardens family will plan around.

programmes.name: MYP 1 to 3, the habit years
programmes.description: Eight subject groups taught through units, with criteria assessed from the start although schools often report in simplified form at this stage. The calendar here is loose, which makes it the right time to build habits rather than chase marks: reading the task instruction, structuring a response, recording process, meeting an internal deadline without a reminder.
programmes.countryNote: Students in these years are home earliest in Discovery Gardens, often by 16:00, with few late commitments. That makes a 16:30 session straightforward, and short sessions twice a week work better than one long one at this age. Nothing in these years is urgent, which is precisely why the habits are cheap to build now.

programmes.name: MYP 4, where the calendar tightens
programmes.description: Criteria are applied at close to full demand, many schools split mathematics into standard and extended routes, and the Personal Project begins in practice even where it is formally an MYP 5 requirement. Reports from this year are the first that genuinely predict Diploma readiness, which makes them worth reading carefully rather than filing.
programmes.countryNote: This is the year Discovery Gardens families most often contact us, usually after an MYP 4 report. It is a good moment, provided the work is timed to the next assessed tasks rather than to the report just received. It is also when the Personal Project goal should be under discussion, a year before most students think about it.

programmes.name: MYP 5, the year with real deadlines
programmes.description: The Personal Project is completed and externally moderated, criteria are assessed at full demand across all subject groups, and some schools enter students for optional on-screen examinations and ePortfolios leading to the IB MYP Certificate. For most students it is also the year of transition into the Diploma or into IGCSE elsewhere.
programmes.countryNote: The Personal Project deadline is the one date in the whole programme that behaves like an examination deadline, and it is the one families most often meet late. Ask the coordinator in September for both the project timeline and whether the school enters eAssessments, because the two together define what MYP 5 support should target.

programmes.name: What MYP 5 leads into
programmes.description: Either the IB Diploma, where criterion-based habits transfer directly into Internal Assessments, or IGCSE at another school, where mark-scheme conventions the Middle Years never taught arrive abruptly. Both transitions are smoother for a student who has learned to show process and answer the task as written.
programmes.countryNote: Families in this corridor frequently change schools at 16, because full IB Diploma provision nearby is thinner than further north. That makes the summer after MYP 5 a genuine planning window rather than a gap, and four to six sessions then costs far less than catching up during a first term at a new school.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-discovery-gardens.subjectsIntro: Each subject group assesses four criteria, and each has its own rhythm of assessed tasks across the year. Knowing the letters is what makes a report actionable.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.description: A knowing and understanding, B investigating patterns, C communicating, D applying mathematics in real-life contexts. Criterion B tasks are usually set as substantial investigations with a known deadline, which makes them the easiest thing in the programme to time support around.

subjects.name: Sciences
subjects.description: A knowing and understanding, B inquiring and designing, C processing and evaluating, D reflecting on the impacts of science. Criteria B and C attach to practical investigations with set deadlines; criterion D is frequently written in the final hour and is worth the same eight marks.

subjects.name: Language and literature
subjects.description: A analysing, B organizing, C producing text, D using language. Assessed through essays and creative tasks spread across the year, so the useful session is the week a task is set rather than after it is returned with a number on it.

subjects.name: Language acquisition
subjects.description: A listening, B reading, C speaking, D writing, assessed within phases rather than year groups. Speaking tasks are scheduled by the school and are the ones students most under-prepare, because fluency under timing needs frequent short practice rather than last-minute revision.

subjects.name: Individuals and societies
subjects.description: A knowing and understanding, B investigating, C communicating, D thinking critically. Criterion B and D tasks are research pieces with deadlines, and criterion D is the strand that separates grades because it asks for evidence weighed rather than summarised.

subjects.name: Design
subjects.description: A inquiring and analysing, B developing ideas, C creating the solution, D evaluating. The process journal carries most of the marks and is kept continuously, which makes this the subject where late help is least effective and early habit-setting most valuable.

subjects.name: Arts
subjects.description: A investigating, B developing, C creating or performing, D evaluating. As in design, documented development is assessed alongside the work. Performance and exhibition dates are fixed well ahead, so the calendar here is unusually visible if anyone looks at it.

subjects.name: Physical and health education
subjects.description: A knowing and understanding, B planning for performance, C applying and performing, D reflecting and improving performance. Written criteria carry real weight, which surprises families who assume the subject is assessed on sporting ability alone.

subjects.name: The Personal Project
subjects.description: Assessed on planning, applying skills and reflecting, with the process record carrying more weight than the product. The one element of the programme with a hard external deadline, and the one most often started too late for the process marks to be available.

subjects.name: Interdisciplinary units
subjects.description: Tasks requiring two subject groups brought together, usually scheduled once or twice a year. Students used to working inside one subject find them disorienting, and the marks go to explaining the connection rather than covering both syllabuses.

subjects.name: Approaches to learning skills
subjects.description: Research, communication, self-management, thinking and social skills, appearing inside criterion descriptors across subject groups. Self-management is the one that most often explains a flat report, and it is a calendar skill rather than an academic one.

subjects.name: Service as action
subjects.description: Service linked to learning with recorded reflection. Not graded as a subject but it appears in reporting, and schools differ in how much documentation they expect, so it is worth asking what your child's school requires and by when.

sections.heading: When criteria are actually assessed, and why reports arrive late
paragraphs: In the Middle Years Programme, assessment happens task by task across the year. A unit culminates in one or more pieces marked against specific criteria out of eight, using published descriptors. Those marks accumulate, and reports present a summary of them converted to a 1 to 7 grade. By the time a parent reads a report, every task behind it has been written, submitted and graded.

That is why reports are a poor trigger for buying support, even though they are the trigger almost everyone uses. The useful question a report answers is which criterion is consistently weaker, which is genuinely valuable. The useless thing a report does is tell you to act now on work that finished weeks ago. Acting on it means acting on the next task, and that requires the school's assessment calendar rather than the report.

Most schools publish or will share a calendar of assessed tasks per subject per term. It is not confidential and it is rarely volunteered to parents. With it, support can be placed in the week a criterion B investigation is set in mathematics, or before a criterion C practical write-up in science, which is when the hour changes the mark rather than commenting on it.

The practical sequence we recommend to Discovery Gardens families is therefore: read the report for the pattern across criteria, ask the school for the assessment calendar for the coming term, then book sessions against the two or three tasks that address the weak criterion. That is usually fewer hours than a weekly arrangement and produces more visible change, because each hour is attached to a mark that has not yet been given.

sections.heading: Reading a report for pattern rather than for grade
paragraphs: A Middle Years report is more informative than it looks, provided you read the criterion detail rather than the headline number. Every subject group assesses four criteria out of eight, and the letters mean different things in different subjects: criterion B is investigating patterns in mathematics and organizing in language and literature. A student with 6 on A and 3 on C in the sciences has a data processing and evaluation problem, not a science problem.

What that shifts is the whole conversation with the school and with any tutor. Instead of asking how to improve in science, the question becomes how criterion C is evidenced and what the descriptor at the 7 to 8 band actually asks for. That is a specific, answerable question, and most subject teachers will engage with it readily because it is the language they assess in.

Patterns across subjects matter too. A student with low criterion C or D marks in several unrelated subject groups is usually showing one issue, not four: process not recorded, reflection written at the last minute, or evidence summarised rather than weighed. That is why hiring four tutors in response to a flat report treats one problem four times at four times the cost.

Self-management is the particular suspect, and it is a calendar skill rather than an academic one. Approaches to learning skills are taught explicitly in the Middle Years and appear inside criterion descriptors. Work that is complete but unplanned, with no process recorded and reflection written in the final hour, scores below the student's understanding in every process-assessed subject simultaneously.

sections.heading: The Personal Project timeline, run properly
paragraphs: The Personal Project is the one element of the Middle Years Programme with a hard external deadline and a formal moderation process, and it is where the calendar matters most. It is completed in MYP 5, supervised in school, and assessed on planning, applying skills and reflecting. The process record carries more weight than the product, which means the marks are earned across months rather than at the end.

The failure pattern is consistent and entirely avoidable. A student picks an ambitious goal, builds something impressive without recording how, and writes the report afterwards from memory. That scores below a modest project with a full process journal, because the available marks are for documented process and cannot be reconstructed. Markers recognise retrospective journals, and six months of decisions cannot be remembered accurately anyway.

Run properly, the project has four phases with different support needs. Goal setting, where feasibility and success criteria are decided and where one hour is worth more than five later. The working phase, where the only thing that matters is whether the journal is being kept. Reflection, where the student evaluates honestly against their own stated criteria. And the report, which should assemble existing material rather than invent it.

The practical instruction for a Discovery Gardens family is to ask the coordinator in September of MYP 4 or MYP 5 for the project timeline, and to book help against the goal-setting phase rather than the report deadline. Most enquiries we receive about Personal Projects arrive in the final term, when the money works least hard and the process marks are already determined.

sections.heading: MYP 5 eAssessments: find out whether your school enters them
paragraphs: Schools differ on this and it changes the whole shape of MYP 5, so it is a question worth asking in September rather than discovering in February. Some schools enter MYP 5 students for optional on-screen examinations and ePortfolios leading to the IB MYP Certificate. Others end the programme with school-assessed criteria and the Personal Project alone. Both are legitimate and they produce different final years.

Where eAssessments are sat, the on-screen examinations reward applying knowledge to unfamiliar stimulus material rather than reproducing taught content. That is a distinct skill, and students who perform well on school assessments and poorly on unseen stimulus are common. The preparation that helps is working with unfamiliar material under timing, which is quite different from revising units.

Where they are not sat, MYP 5 ends with the Personal Project as its only externally moderated element, and the useful focus becomes the transition ahead. For students continuing into the Diploma that means the habits Internal Assessments assume: stating a method, processing data, documenting a process, evaluating honestly. For students moving to IGCSE elsewhere it means mark-scheme conventions the Middle Years never taught.

That second case is specific to this corridor and worth naming. Full IB Diploma provision in the Jebel Ali and Dubai South area is thinner than further north, so a number of Discovery Gardens families change schools at 16 and some change curriculum as well. Knowing in September which of those two futures applies is what makes MYP 5 support targeted rather than general.

sections.heading: Ramadan and the UAE year at Middle Years level
paragraphs: The UAE academic year runs from late summer to early summer with a winter break and a spring break, and Ramadan moves roughly eleven days earlier each Gregorian year. In recent years it has fallen in the spring term. Schools operate reduced hours during it, which changes the shape of a student's day and, at Middle Years level, often coincides with a cluster of assessed tasks before the end of the year.

The adjustments are easier at this stage than in an examination year, and worth making deliberately. Reduced school hours free earlier afternoon slots, which suits younger students who concentrate better before dinner anyway. Energy patterns change for fasting students, so a session that worked at 17:00 may work better at 19:30, or the reverse, and it is a question to ask rather than an assumption to make.

Where this interacts with the calendar is in task deadlines. If assessed tasks fall in or immediately after Ramadan, the planning for them should happen before it starts rather than during it. A criterion B investigation set during a period of reduced hours and shortened concentration is exactly the task that gets produced hurriedly, with the process record skipped, which costs marks in the strand that rewards process.

The simple protection is to agree at the outset that the session slot will move during Ramadan and across the breaks, rather than discovering that it no longer works and letting the arrangement lapse. At Middle Years level a lapsed arrangement is particularly easy to leave lapsed, because nothing looks urgent, and that is how a year passes without the criterion problem being addressed.

sections.heading: The two-year run into the Diploma or into IGCSE
paragraphs: MYP 4 and MYP 5 are, in practice, a two-year run-up to something quite different, and what that something is should shape them. For a student continuing into the IB Diploma, the Middle Years criteria are preparation in the most literal sense: stating a method, processing data, documenting a process and evaluating honestly are precisely what every Diploma Internal Assessment will later require.

That makes criterion-focused work in MYP 4 and 5 the cheapest Diploma preparation available. A student who arrives in Diploma 1 able to read a criterion and produce evidence against it needs one weekly session; a student who arrives without that habit needs a block in every subject at exactly the moment when every family in Dubai is competing for the same specialists in the same evening slots.

For a student moving to IGCSE at another school, the run-up is almost the opposite. The Middle Years does not teach method marks, command terms or writing to a time limit, because it does not assess that way. Those arrive abruptly in Year 10 or Year 11 at the new school, and a student who has only ever been assessed against criteria can be strong academically and weak on the paper.

So the two futures need different final years, and that is the single most useful planning distinction at this stage. A family that knows in MYP 4 which route is likely can use MYP 5 to build towards it. A family that decides late gets a generic MYP 5 and a harder first term wherever the student lands, which is avoidable with one conversation and a calendar.

sections.heading: Where in the year to intervene for each kind of problem
paragraphs: Different criterion problems have different best moments, which is the practical pay-off of treating the Middle Years as a calendar. A content gap can be addressed at any point, because content recurs. A criteria-reading problem should be addressed in the week a task is set, because that is when the descriptors can still change what gets produced. Those two are frequently confused and the confusion wastes most of the money spent at this stage.

A process-documentation problem, which affects design, the arts, the sciences and the Personal Project, has to be addressed at the start of a piece of work. Nobody can document a process retrospectively in a way that scores, and markers are experienced at spotting attempts. So that intervention belongs in the first week of a unit or project, and it is one of the few things in this programme that genuinely cannot be done later.

A reflection problem is slightly more forgiving, since reflection is written towards the end of a task, but it still needs to be taught before the student writes it rather than after it is marked. One session explaining what evaluation asks for, as distinct from description or apology, usually changes the next three pieces of work across several subjects at once.

A self-management problem is a year-round intervention and the one most worth starting in MYP 1 to 3, when nothing is urgent. It is also the one families least often recognise, because it presents as a flat report across subjects rather than as a weakness in any of them. Treating it as four subject problems is the most expensive diagnostic error available at this stage.

sections.heading: What a Middle Years tutor will not do, and our limits
paragraphs: Because the Middle Years is assessed almost entirely on work produced in school, the boundary on help sits at the centre of the arrangement rather than at its edge. An IB Gram tutor reads criteria with the student, questions a plan or a goal, teaches technique, demonstrates method, gives written feedback on the student's own work and records what was covered. That is the territory, and most of the available marks in this programme sit inside it.

What a tutor will not do is produce work for submission. No written tasks, no Personal Project content, no process journal entries, no completed investigations, and no outlines for a student to fill in. At least one provider in this market sells completed internal assessments at a fixed price, and submitted work that is not the student's own is malpractice, with the exposure falling on the student rather than on the seller.

We also do not reproduce or distribute IB subject guides, task banks or assessment criteria documents as downloads. Criteria are discussed and explained, and sessions work from the task sheets and marked work the school has issued, which is the better basis in any case because it is what the student is actually being assessed against.

Two further limits. We do not predict or guarantee grades, including criterion scores, and any provider doing so is selling confidence rather than teaching. And we hold no approval, accreditation or partnership from the IB, KHDA, ADEK, SPEA or the Ministry of Education; we explain what those bodies do and claim nothing from them. Lessons run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, and no tutor attends a UAE address.

process.title: Send a marked task and the next deadline
process.description: The marked task shows which criterion strand was missed; the next deadline shows when a session can still change something. Add the subject group, the MYP year and the earliest time your child is at the desk. Students here are often home by 16:00, which makes 16:30 workable.

process.title: Ask the school for the assessment calendar
process.description: Most schools will share a term's assessed tasks per subject. It is rarely volunteered and it is what turns a report into a plan, because it lets support land in the week a task is set rather than two weeks after one was graded.

process.title: We match by subject group and name the tutor
process.description: You are told who will teach and whether they work to the four criteria in that subject group. Ask them to name the criteria; it takes ten seconds and is the clearest test available. If we cannot match the subject group we say so rather than offering a general subject tutor.

process.title: Free diagnosis session on the marked work
process.description: Forty to sixty minutes reading the task against the strand descriptors, ending with a specific statement of which criterion is costing marks and why. No payment and no obligation. Many families here use this session alone and then talk to the subject teacher.

process.title: Book against tasks, not against a rhythm
process.description: Sessions placed in the weeks assessed tasks are set, rather than a fixed weekly hour regardless of what is happening. That usually means fewer hours with more visible effect, because each one attaches to a mark that has not yet been awarded.

process.title: Ask about MYP 5 and the Personal Project in September
process.description: Whether the school enters eAssessments, and the Personal Project timeline. Those two answers define what the final Middle Years year should target, and both are easy to get in September and impossible to act on in February.

whyPoints.title: Timed to the assessment cycle
whyPoints.description: Criteria are assessed task by task, so a session in the week a task is set changes a mark while a session after a report comments on one. We ask for the next deadline before anything else, because that is what decides whether an hour can achieve something.

whyPoints.title: Reports read for pattern, not grade
whyPoints.description: Four criteria out of eight per subject group, with the same letter meaning different things in different subjects. A 6 on A and a 3 on C in the sciences is a processing and evaluation problem, which is a specific and answerable question rather than a general one.

whyPoints.title: Process documentation addressed at the start
whyPoints.description: Process marks cannot be earned retrospectively, in design, the arts, the sciences or the Personal Project. We put that intervention in the first week of a unit or project, because it is one of the few things in this programme that genuinely cannot be done later.

whyPoints.title: The Personal Project split into two blocks
whyPoints.description: Three sessions on the goal and the process record, then two or three on reflection and the report. That matches the project's own timeline, rather than arriving in the final term when the process marks are already determined.

whyPoints.title: The destination used to shape MYP 5
whyPoints.description: A student heading for the Diploma needs criterion habits; a student moving to IGCSE needs method marks and command terms, which the Middle Years never teaches. Knowing which applies in MYP 4 makes the final year targeted rather than generic.

whyPoints.title: Fewer hours, better placed
whyPoints.description: Most of this page argues for less tutoring rather than more: a diagnosis session, then sessions attached to specific tasks. At Middle Years level that regularly outperforms a standing weekly hour bought in response to a report.

faqs.question: With no external exams until the end, which dates should a parent be tracking?
faqs.answer: The assessment cycle. Criteria are assessed task by task across the year, with each task marked out of eight against published descriptors, and those marks accumulate into the reported grade. So there are deadlines constantly, they are just internal. The Personal Project in MYP 5 has a hard external deadline and is moderated. Ask the school for the calendar of assessed tasks per subject per term; it is rarely volunteered and it is what makes support plannable.

faqs.question: Why is a report a poor moment to start tutoring?
faqs.answer: Because every task behind it has already been written, submitted and graded. A report is genuinely useful for identifying which criterion is consistently weaker, which is a real diagnosis. What it cannot do is give you something to act on, because the marks it summarises are fixed. Acting means acting on the next assessed task, and that requires the assessment calendar rather than the report. The same money placed before a task does far more than after one.

faqs.question: What does my child's criterion mark pattern actually tell me?
faqs.answer: More than the grade does. Each subject group assesses four criteria out of eight and the letters mean different things in different subjects: criterion B is investigating patterns in mathematics and organizing in language and literature. A 6 on criterion A and a 3 on criterion C in the sciences is a data processing and evaluation problem rather than a science problem. That turns the conversation with the teacher into a specific question about a strand descriptor.

faqs.question: When should Personal Project support be booked?
faqs.answer: At goal setting, which is usually a year before most families think about it, and then again at reflection. The process record carries more weight than the product, and marks for documented decisions cannot be earned retrospectively. One hour spent on whether the goal is achievable and documentable, and what success will look like, protects more marks than five hours on the report. Most enquiries we receive arrive in the final term, when the process marks are already determined.

faqs.question: What question about the IB MYP Certificate should we put to the coordinator?
faqs.answer: Ask the coordinator in September, because schools differ and it changes the whole shape of the final year. Where the optional on-screen examinations and ePortfolios leading to the IB MYP Certificate are entered, the examinations reward applying knowledge to unfamiliar stimulus material rather than reproducing taught content, so preparation means unseen material under timing. Where they are not, the Personal Project is the only externally moderated element and MYP 5 support should target the transition ahead instead.

faqs.question: My child's whole report is middling. Do we need four tutors?
faqs.answer: Almost certainly not. Low criterion C or D marks across several unrelated subject groups usually indicate one issue rather than four: process not recorded, reflection written at the last minute, or evidence summarised rather than weighed. Self-management is the particular suspect, and it is a calendar skill rather than an academic one. One diagnosis session on two marked tasks from different subjects normally finds the common cause, which is far cheaper than treating it four times.

faqs.question: How does Ramadan affect Middle Years work in Dubai?
faqs.answer: It shifts roughly eleven days earlier each Gregorian year and in recent years has fallen in the spring term, with UAE schools operating reduced hours. That frees earlier afternoon slots, which suits younger students who concentrate better before dinner, and it changes energy patterns for fasting students. The planning point is task deadlines: a criterion B investigation set during reduced hours tends to be produced hurriedly with the process record skipped, so plan for it before Ramadan starts.

faqs.question: Which criterion problems genuinely cannot be fixed later?
faqs.answer: Process documentation. In design, the arts, the sciences and the Personal Project, marks are available for a recorded process, and nobody can reconstruct six months of decisions in a way that scores. Markers are experienced at recognising retrospective journals. So that intervention belongs in the first week of a unit or project. Content gaps, by contrast, can be addressed at almost any point because content recurs, and criteria-reading problems need the week a task is set.

faqs.question: What should MYP 4 and MYP 5 be building towards?
faqs.answer: It depends on the destination, which is the most useful planning distinction at this stage. A student continuing into the IB Diploma needs criterion habits, because stating a method, processing data, documenting a process and evaluating honestly are exactly what Internal Assessments require. A student moving to IGCSE at another school needs method marks, command terms and timed writing, none of which the Middle Years teaches because it does not assess that way.

faqs.question: What time do MYP sessions run for families in Discovery Gardens?
faqs.answer: 16:30 is the common slot, and 15:50 for students on the nearest Dubai Investments Park routes. Discovery Gardens is compact, so pickup is quicker than in the villa communities nearby, and Middle Years students have fewer late commitments than their Diploma siblings. Sessions run to 21:30 Gulf Standard Time. For younger Middle Years students two forty-five minute sessions a week work better than one long one, because concentration rather than content is the limit at that age.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with a task that is due this week?
faqs.answer: Yes, within a firm boundary. A tutor can read the criteria with your child against the task sheet, question their plan, teach the technique the task needs, and give written feedback on what your child has already drafted. A tutor cannot write any part of it, dictate it, or outline it for your child to fill in. If the deadline is tomorrow and nothing has been started, the honest answer is that the session will help the next task more than this one.

faqs.question: Is it worth paying for MYP support when nothing feels urgent?
faqs.answer: That is exactly when it is cheapest and most effective. In MYP 1 to 3 the calendar is loose, which makes it the right time to build habits: reading the task instruction, structuring a response, recording process, meeting an internal deadline without a reminder. Those habits are what Diploma Internal Assessments later assume. A student who arrives in Diploma 1 without them needs a block in every subject at the busiest point in the Dubai tutoring year.

faqs.question: What is the difference between criterion D in science and in individuals and societies?
faqs.answer: In the sciences, criterion D is reflecting on the impacts of science, and it is frequently written in the final hour despite being worth the same eight marks as the other three strands. In individuals and societies, criterion D is thinking critically, which asks for evidence and arguments weighed rather than summarised, and it is the strand that most separates grades. Same letter, different demand, which is why knowing the letters for your child's specific subjects matters.

faqs.question: How many sessions does a Middle Years problem usually need?
faqs.answer: Fewer than families expect, if they are well placed. A diagnosis session on marked work, then two or three attached to specific upcoming tasks, resolves most single-criterion problems. A process-documentation habit takes one session to establish and then needs checking once. The arrangements that run for a whole year without visible change are usually weekly hours bought in response to a report and spent revising content that was never the problem.

faqs.question: What should we do in the summer after MYP 5?
faqs.answer: Target the actual destination rather than revising generally. For a student entering the IB Diploma, four to six sessions on the habits Internal Assessments assume: stating a method, processing data, documenting process, evaluating honestly. For a student moving to IGCSE at a new school, the same number on method marks, command terms and writing to a time limit. It is the quietest period in the Dubai tutoring year, so specialist availability is at its widest.

faqs.question: Can you guarantee my child's criterion marks will improve?
faqs.answer: No, and we do not guarantee grades or criterion scores in any subject. What can be stated is where the marks are available and when they are reachable: criteria read before a task is produced, process documented from the first week, reflection taught before it is written, and self-management addressed year-round. A provider promising a specific criterion improvement is selling confidence. The honest version of this service is placing a small number of hours where the calendar still allows them to matter.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-discovery-gardens.closingHeading: Send a marked task and the date of the next one
dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-discovery-gardens.closingBody: An IB MYP tutor in Discovery Gardens is worth booking when the hour can still change a mark. Send a marked task rather than a report, the subject group, the MYP year, and the date the next assessed task is due. Ask the school for the term's assessment calendar and the Personal Project timeline while you are at it. We will match a tutor who works to the four criteria in that subject, run a free diagnosis session reading the task against the strand descriptors, and tell you honestly how many sessions the problem needs. Lessons run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-downtown-dubai.tutorsIntro: These tutors teach MYP subjects at Years 7 to 11, which in IB terms is MYP 2 to MYP 5. The requests that arrive most from the central corridor are sciences criterion B and C, mathematics criterion B, and Personal Project process coaching in MYP 5.

intro.heading: A report card of fours and fives, and a school run that leaves no time to fix it
paragraphs: The Middle Years Programme reports differently from every other system a Downtown family is likely to have come from, and that difference causes most of the confusion. There are no percentages. Each subject is assessed against four criteria, labelled A to D, each marked out of eight. Those four marks are added and converted through a published boundary table into a single grade from 1 to 7. A child can score 7 on criterion A and 3 on criterion B and come out with a 5 overall, and a parent reading that 5 has no idea that the problem is entirely in one skill.

This matters more in Dubai than it might elsewhere, because MYP students here are often the same students who will be choosing between the IB Diploma, A Levels and an IGCSE route within two or three years. The criteria are not arbitrary school policy; they are the skills the Diploma will assess under different names. Criterion B in MYP Sciences is inquiring and designing, and it becomes Research design in the DP Scientific Investigation. Criterion B in MYP Mathematics is investigating patterns, and it becomes most of the mathematical exploration. A child who is weak on one criterion at thirteen is weak on the same thing at seventeen, with more riding on it.

The Downtown constraint is time. No private school sits inside the district, so every child here is bussed out: north towards Al Safa and Al Satwa, east over the creek to Oud Metha and Al Garhoud, or south-east to Sobha Hartland, Meydan and Nad Al Sheba. The morning pickup is between about 6.40am and 7.15am. The return is between 3.45pm and 5.00pm depending on the corridor, and two afternoons a week usually carry a co-curricular commitment. An MYP 4 student has homework from eight subject groups and a long day behind them.

That combination is why MYP tuition in this district fails when it is unfocused and works when it is narrow. Teaching an MYP student more content is rarely the answer, because the content is not usually the problem. Teaching them how criterion C in individuals and societies wants a source handled, or how criterion B in mathematics wants a pattern described and then generalised, is a small and specific job. It takes four or five sessions per criterion and the mark moves visibly, which is also what makes a twelve-year-old believe the effort was worth it.

Lessons run live online from the apartment, at an hour set by the bus rather than by a tutor's commute. The practical effect is that a session can start at 5.15pm on a short-run Tuesday and 6.15pm on a long-run Thursday, and that nobody loses forty minutes each way on Al Khail Road. IB Gram does not run home visits anywhere in the UAE; home tutoring is a service we offer only in India, and that is stated here rather than discovered at booking.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-downtown-dubai.programmesIntro: The Middle Years Programme spans five years and three school phases, and what a tutor should be doing changes completely across them. These are the stages Downtown families ask about, and what each one needs.

programmes.name: MYP 1-2, the first two years
programmes.description: The first contact with criterion-based assessment, usually after a Primary Years Programme or a national system that used percentages. Students are learning what a command term means and what a criterion descriptor is actually asking for. The useful tutoring here is study skills and assessment literacy, not subject content, because the content is not yet hard.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai this stage often coincides with a family arriving from another country, so a child meets criterion marking and a new school system in the same term. A short block of sessions focused on reading a task sheet properly resolves more of that than subject teaching does.

programmes.name: MYP 3-4, where the gap opens
programmes.description: Content depth increases across all eight subject groups at once and the interdisciplinary demands rise. This is where a single weak criterion starts to show up in several subjects simultaneously, because criterion C in most subject groups is about communicating and criterion D is about critical application. A student who cannot structure an extended written response is marked down four times over.
programmes.countryNote: Downtown and Business Bay families most often seek MYP help at this stage, and the trigger is usually a report where the grades dropped by one across several subjects at once. That pattern almost always points at a shared skill rather than at five separate content problems.

programmes.name: MYP 5 and the Personal Project
programmes.description: The final MYP year carries the Personal Project, a substantial independent piece documented in a process journal and reported against published criteria, plus any on-screen examinations and ePortfolios the school enters students for. Students who have coasted on content recall meet a project that rewards planning, evidence of process and honest self-assessment.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai, MYP 5 is also the year the post-16 decision is made between the IB Diploma and an A Level route, often at a different school. Project deadlines and option deadlines collide, and a tutor's most useful contribution is frequently helping a student protect project time rather than teaching anything.

programmes.name: What MYP leads into
programmes.description: The Diploma Programme assesses six subjects plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. MYP criteria map onto DP assessment closely but not obviously: inquiring and designing becomes Research design in a science investigation, investigating patterns becomes most of the mathematical exploration, and the Personal Project's process journal is the direct ancestor of the Extended Essay's researcher's reflection space.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai students moving from MYP into DP at the same school find the administration smooth and the assessment jarring. The grade scale looks identical, 1 to 7, but it is reached a different way: MYP adds criterion marks, DP weights examination papers. That difference is worth explaining to a student in MYP 5 rather than in DP1.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-downtown-dubai.subjectsIntro: MYP requests from the central corridor cluster in a few subject groups, usually because of one criterion rather than the whole subject. These are the ones we are asked for most, with the criterion that is normally the real problem.

subjects.name: Sciences
subjects.description: Criteria are knowing and understanding, inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating, and reflecting on the impacts of science. The usual losses are in criterion B, where a hypothesis has no justified variable range, and criterion C, where data is tabulated but never properly processed.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.description: Criteria are knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts. Criterion B is the one that separates students: describing a pattern earns little, generalising it and then justifying the generalisation earns the top band.

subjects.name: Individuals and Societies
subjects.description: Criteria are knowing and understanding, investigating, communicating, and thinking critically. Criterion D is where marks are lost most, because students summarise sources accurately and never evaluate their origin, purpose or limitations, which is what the descriptor actually asks for.

subjects.name: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Criteria are analysing, organising, producing text, and using language. The commonest issue is criterion A: a student retells the plot instead of analysing how a writer achieves an effect, which is the same gap that limits DP English Paper 1 later.

subjects.name: Language Acquisition
subjects.description: Assessed in phases rather than year groups, across listening, reading, speaking and writing. Dubai students often sit in a phase that no longer matches their ability because placement happened on arrival. A phase check is worth doing before any tutoring is planned.

subjects.name: Design
subjects.description: Criteria are inquiring and analysing, developing ideas, creating the solution, and evaluating. Design marks reward documented iteration, which students resist because it feels like paperwork. The habit it builds is the one the Personal Project rewards a year or two later.

subjects.name: Arts
subjects.description: Assessed through a process portfolio as well as a finished product, with criteria covering knowing and understanding, developing skills, thinking creatively and responding. Students who produce strong work and document nothing lose marks they have genuinely earned elsewhere.

subjects.name: Physical and Health Education
subjects.description: Includes a written and reflective component alongside performance, which surprises families who expect a practical subject. The planning and reflection criteria are where the grade is usually decided, and both are coachable at a desk.

subjects.name: Arabic
subjects.description: Taken both as a language acquisition subject and as a KHDA requirement for schools in Dubai. Written and oral assessment rewards drilled structures more than vocabulary breadth, and separate streams exist for Arab and non-Arab students.

subjects.name: Personal Project
subjects.description: An independent project documented in a process journal and reported against published criteria. Marks are lost on evidence of process rather than on the product, because students build something good and record almost nothing about how they decided to build it.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-downtown-dubai.regionsIntro: Downtown Dubai heads a dense central corridor whose families use the same schools and the same roads. The timing arithmetic below applies across all of these districts with the drive times adjusted.

regions.name: Downtown Dubai
regions.note: Boulevard towers and Old Town low-rises, served by Burj Khalifa/Dubai Mall metro. No school inside the district, which is why every MYP timetable here starts with a bus.

regions.name: Business Bay
regions.note: South across the Dubai Canal with its own metro station. The same campuses serve both districts, and pickups here run slightly later, pushing the evening slot back by half an hour.

regions.name: DIFC
regions.note: A financial free zone with a separate court system, though schools remain under KHDA. Parents working in the towers above commonly need sessions after 7pm, which suits MYP students less than DP students.

regions.name: Sobha Hartland
regions.note: A school destination rather than a commute origin, with both IB continuum and British campuses. A large share of Downtown's southbound buses terminate here.

regions.name: Al Jaddaf and Culture Village
regions.note: Creek-side communities with a short school run and an IB school within ten minutes. MYP families here report the earliest home arrivals in the corridor.

regions.name: Meydan and Nad Al Sheba
regions.note: Villa districts whose schools draw from Downtown apartments. The afternoon return along Al Khail Road is slow, so MYP students on this route are rarely settled before 5.15pm.

regions.name: Mohammed Bin Rashid City
regions.note: New villa developments between Meydan and Al Quoz, with schools opening into the area. Year groups here change size and composition between cohorts more than elsewhere.

regions.name: Al Quoz and Al Quoz 4
regions.note: Mixed residential and industrial, with several long-established schools. Afternoon traffic from Al Quoz back towards the Boulevard is the worst leg in the corridor.

schoolClusters.city: IB continuum campuses within reach of Downtown
schoolClusters.note: Schools running the Primary Years and Middle Years Programmes, some continuing into the Diploma on the same campus. These generate most of the MYP enquiries from Downtown, Business Bay and DIFC, and their reporting conventions are where the criterion confusion starts.

schoolClusters.city: Mixed-programme and British campuses nearby
schoolClusters.note: Schools in Hartland, Meydan and Al Safa that run British curriculum routes, sometimes alongside IB programmes. Families in this corridor often compare an MYP route against an IGCSE route using these campuses, which is a real decision rather than a hypothetical one.

schoolClusters.note: The Oud Metha, Al Garhoud and Al Jaddaf belt, around twenty minutes from the Boulevard outside peak hours. A mix of curricula, and some of the longest-established school communities in the city.
